speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of both urgent and pressing necessity, which is non-partisan in nature. The Pan-American Wheelchair Games scheduled for Halifax next month, involving some 500 wheelchair athletes from 17 countries, are threatened with cancellation due to rules limiting the number of wheelchair passengers who may be carried on commercial aircraft in Canada. That the government, while recognizing that it must ensure safety in the event of evacuation, take whatever steps possible to assist in providing appropriate transportation to fly the 500 wheelchair athletes to the Pan-American Wheelchair Games in Halifax.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. Canadian productivity in all commercial industries, measured in production per manhour, increased, on average, between the years 1967 and 1971 by 4.2 per cent a year; by 2.6 per cent a year between 1972 and 1976; by 0.9 per cent a year between 1977 and 1981; and by 0.2 per cent last year, a very, very serious drop in productivity. Would the Prime Minister reconsider the negative answer he gave to me a couple of weeks ago in this House on this very important matter and, instead, give serious consideration to providing generous tax incentives, to be paid in direct proportion to increases in productivity, so that Canadian producers can find it practical and worth their while to buy the new machinery, plant and production systems necessary to increase productivity, and thereby lower costs and selling prices, and in this way, increase sales, production and jobs?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TAX INCENTIVES TO STIMULATE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is at it again with his remarks that productivity in Canada has dropped. The fact is, and I have told him this before, that productivity has dropped in most industrialized countries, and economists are trying to analyse the many reasons for this slowdown. Most people agree that it is at least partly due to a restructuring of our economies as a result of the OPEC or energy crisis. Indeed, the statistics quoted by the hon. member appear to indicate that the slowdown has been particularly visible since the OPEC crisis in 1973.
Regarding the hon. member's suggestion that further tax incentives be introduced, I would remind him that these measures have been adequate in the past, before we got into a recessionary period. Of course, all countries are now suffering from the recession we are experiencing today, and there is reason to believe that when we get out of this recession, the Canadian tax system, which is basically more generous to business than the American system, will again have a positive effect and that productivity will increase.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, July 19, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-125, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and the amendment of Mr. Clark (p. 19456).

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is asking under the present borrowing authority for what amounts to a $4 billion slush fund. This is over and above the amount of money required to run the government this year as has been projected. The government projected financial requirements in the amount of $17.1 billion for this year. It has already had $10.2 billion in borrowing authority this year and it also has $3.6 billion in unused authority from previous years. Bill C-125 proposes to give the government an additional $11 billion.
As a businessman I recognize the need for borrowing and the need to pay bills and accounts. But I also know that if I walked into my bank and asked for a borrowing requirement of $17,000 and I told the bank: "Just for the fun of it I want a little bit of a slush fund, so lend me $21,000", the bank would tear up my loan application.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: They would give it to you.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
An hon. member on the other side says the bank would give me the money. Hon. members over there are not bankers; you can certainly tell that, Mr. Speaker.
If a small-business man went into a bank for a loan, he would show the bank his requirements. Take, for example, a small-business man who asked his bank for a loan of $1.7 million but said to his banker: "Mr. Banker, that is the requirement but 1 want $2.1 million because I need a $400,000 slush fund in case something goes wrong." The banker would certainly throw him out of the door. The banker would tell him that he did not know what he was doing and that he did not know how to run his business.
If I were responsible for a public company and as president went to the board of directors asking for the same kind of borrowing with a slush fund attached to it, the chairman and some member of that board would move a motion of nonconfidence and say to me: "Mr. President, get out; you do not know what you are doing."
The people of Canada are saying, and they are saying the same thing to their representatives in this House, that this government does not know what it is doing when it asks this House to approve a $4 billion slush fund. This is a way for the government to avoid its responsibilities and its accountability to the people of Canada through this very important green room.
During the past two years that I have been here, we have continually seen a hiding from the public of what the plans of the government are and what the government is going to do. We have seen a blue ribbon committee appointed. This committee has been appointed to discuss a budget that was brought into this House and introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). The budget may be changed as a result of the findings of this committee. The government is treating the budget as a white paper. The government is treating the budget as a document that has not been tabled in this House of Commons as a budget or a plan of operation for the country. The government has done it to the exclusion of every member in this House, including its own backbenchers. In fact, the government's backbenchers are being treated shoddily. They are treated worse than the government treats the opposition benches.
Every time I pick up a newspaper or a magazine I see the following kinds of headlines: "Canada's economy in decline; Canada's economy is now in crisis; Crisis situation faces Canada; Canada in severe recession; Worst unemployment facing Canadians since the dirty thirties". These are the headlines that we read every day. What about these: "Is it a depression? Canada faces sick economy; bankruptcies at an all-time high; investment at an all-time low"?
Then we read what the very cavalier Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the very arrogant Prime Minister of this country, says: "We have had the hell scared out of us." The Prime Minister should not be saying that. He should be saying: "The Liberals under me have scared the hell out of Canadians right across the country." The Liberals have created a Canadian nightmare.
Yesterday in this House, I asked a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). I pointed out to him what the national energy policy had done to the country. And what was his reply? The minister said: "I am not responsible for that member's nightmares." I was only telling the minister what is happening. To get a reply like that to a very legitimate question to him shows the arrogance of this government, a government that can come into this chamber and arrogantly place before this House of Commons an order-an act-requesting or saying-because the government knows it will be able to pass the bill-that it wants a $4 billion slush fund. The situation is absolutely ludicrous.
I ask all hon. members to reflect for a moment on why in this country, with our vast, abundant resources, with our natural God-given resources, with our wealth, our highly educated work force, a very highly productive work force, a
July 20, 1982

highly skilled work force, with people who desire to get out and build our country, we are in the economic mess that we face today. We have everything going for us, Mr. Speaker. Why has the economy gone the way it has? Why is unemployment at an all-time high? Why are bankruptcies at an all-time high? Why do companies have liquidity problems? Why are workers being laid off every day? Why do we have people frightened that they will lose their homes? Why are people feeling threatened with the loss of their life savings? Why are all these things happening?
What do we hear in our debates? We hear from government members that it is because of world conditions. We hear the Prime Minister say it is all a result of world conditions. We hear the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources say the same thing. We hear the Minister of Finance say it is because of world conditions or it is because of the situation in the United States. We also hear that it is because of Reaganomics. That is what we hear from the red rump, the New Democratic Party, the "Liberal Party west". We hear about Reaganomics and that it is Reagan in the United States who is causing all of this mess. We hear that our problems are caused by the United States high interest rate policy, and because the U.S. economy is not moving, ours cannot move.
Then we hear other members say that our problems are caused by a lazy work force and that Canadians are not productive. The Prime Minister has the audacity to stand up and say that Canadians' expectations are too high, that Canadians have to bring the level of their expectations down. We have heard him say that Canadians have been living off the fat of the land for too long and Canadians now will have to tighten their belts.
Those are the kinds of things we hear. We hear that Canada's problems are the fault of unions, that union demands have been too high. Then we hear the problems being blamed on civil servants and that their wage increase will be held to 6 per cent this year. But most of all we hear the problems being blamed on the general public, because it wants too much and wants too much for nothing.
I agree there is a general downturn in world economy which is bound to affect to a degree what is happening here in Canada. I agree that our economy is tied closely to that of the United States and that as a result we in Canada are going to feel the effects of an economic downturn in the United States. Certainly that happens, but of all the countries in the western world, Canada is the best equipped to face an economic downturn. Why are we not facing it? Why are we not surviving the economic downturn? Why are we not a model for the rest of the world? It is because of lack of trust and confidence.
For 30 unprecedented years Canada was looked upon worldwide as the place in which to invest. Canada was looked upon as having a stable government; it was the land of opportunity. When people in European money markets talked about investing in the new world, Canada was the place to go because it had a stable political climate. It was the land of the future.
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Do my hon. friends remember ten years ago when the Prime Minister said that the eighties belonged to Canada, that the next two decades were ours, that we would become a world leader? Well, we have become a world leader! We have become a showplace for the rest of the world to look at as an example of how not to run a country, of how not to rob from every individual in the country to run a bureaucracy like we have in Canada.
My hon. friends should read the publications of respected economists in Great Britain. They should read what they have to say about the Canadian economy. It will make them ashamed. They should read what has been written in German and French publications. I am talking about publications in France. They should read what they say in the European Economic Community. Canada has now been relegated to the position of a Third World country for investment opportunities, with an unstable government, a government which cannot keep its promises, a government which will say one thing one year and change its mind the next.
Let us look at the confidence which the government inspired with the national energy policy. It was outright theft of investment. We in Canada have always had a policy of inviting foreign investment into the country and of saying to investors: "Please come in and help us develop our resources. Please come in, these are the kinds of things we will give you: we will allow you to write off some of your investment against income". Various incentives were put in place.
The very first budget introduced in the House of Commons by the Minister of Finance was in the disguise of a national energy policy. It was disguised document. It was a document which actually stole; it was out and out theft of interest and investments of foreign companies. The government might just as well have come forward and confiscated entire companies. Every large investor, every foreign investor in Canada, saw what the national energy policy was doing. It was clearly the most shameful document to come before the House of Commons in the two years I have been here.
What was the result? Well, investment flow stopped. There was no more investment by foreigners in Canada. They said that they could not trust Canadians. They do not look solely at the Prime Minister, the National Energy Program, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance or the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley). They also look at Canada and say that Canadians can no longer be trusted because they have elected an unstable government which does not keep its word.
I have roamed the world. I represented Canada in the armed forces overseas. I was proud to walk down the streets with the inscription "Canada" on my shoulders. I was proud, but I do not have that pride today when I visit the United States or Europe. Do hon. members remember when we all used to wear little lapel pins depicting the Canadian flag so that everyone would know that we were Canadian? Many Canadians are not wearing them now because they know that the government stole investment from people who took us at our word when they were promised a stable climate for investment.

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
What has been the result? There has been a vast outflow of investment capital from Canada which is needed to develop our resources. It has gone to other countries. It has created a drain on our Canadian dollar. Immediately when that happens, our Canadian dollar gets weak. Then to keep the dollar from getting weaker and weaker, which contributes to inflation, the government in its wisdom must raise interest rates for shortterm borrowing to attract money back. The interest rate which we pay on investment coming to Canada is a reflection of how the investment community views the country.
We all know what first and second mortgages are. Do hon. members remember the days when we could obtain first mortgages for 12 per cent and second mortgages, because they were a little more risky, were available at 15 per cent or 20 per cent? We all knew if we went to finance companies to finance a car that they would look at our credit rating. We all knew that they would look at us as individuals and say: "Yes, he gets a preferred rate." It might have been 2 per cent or 3 per cent cheaper than the next man walking in the door who wanted to buy a car, because he was not as trustworthy and, therefore, had to pay more for his loan to finance his purchase. As a result of the national energy policy we are paying more to finance our country because the investment community no longer trusts Canadians, the Canadian government or the Canadian investment climate.
One country which has always been very similar to ours is Australia. It is much like Canada, a vast country, nearly as large as Canada, except for the Northwest Territories. It has a population of somewhere between 12 million and 13 million people. It is extremely nationalistic. Australia is as nationalistic as Canada, but it recognizes something which our government has failed to recognize, that the domestic supply of investment capital is not adequate. We do not have enough domestic supply of investment capital to develop resources in Canada to create a strong country. The Australians are very pragmatic. They have rolled out the welcome mat for foreign investment.
Let me turn to a list of names to see whether hon. members recognize them. They are: Carling O'Keefe Ltd., Canada Northwest Land Ltd., Coho Resources Ltd., Consolidated Live Star Resources Ltd., Hiram Walker Resources Ltd., Hudson's Bay Oil & Gas Co. Ltd., Medcon Resources Ltd., Norcen Energy Resources Ltd., Nu-West Group Ltd., Oakwood Petroleum Ltd., Ocelot Industries Ltd., PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd., Ranger Oil (Canada) Ltd., Sulpetro Ltd., United Canso Oil & Gas Ltd., Westburne International Industries Ltd., and Silverton Resources Ltd. Every one of those companies are Canadian companies which moved down to Australia during the past two years because of the economic climate, investment climate and political climate there. All told, there is approximately 30 Canadian companies operating in Australia at the present time with in excess of 1,000 Canadian geologists and approximately 2,000 well-trained rig operators, derrick men and floor men searching for oil and natural gas. And we wonder where the boys went? They did
not all go to the United States; many of them went to Australia.
These 30 companies were lost to Canada because we have a national energy policy in the guise of a budget, which virtually destroyed an industry. Australia has laid out the welcome mat. Mr. William Nixon, a Canadian, president of Medcon Resources has said that it is one of the last places where you have political stability and vast areas of relatively unexplored and interesting rock to play with. In other words, he is an entrepreneur who wants to discover and actively produce those resources. That man was driven from Canada.
I will quote another example. I have a report which says that the Australian government-
-staunchly supports both free enterprise and energy development. And, while the Fraser government as a whole is nationalist-minded, it's also pragmatic.
It recognizes that the domestic capital is just not there. Therefore, it has put out the welcome mat.
Another example concerns exploration permits in Australia which would make you think you were reading about Canada 10 or 15 years ago when articles of this type were written about Canada. They are now being written about Australia with Canadian players. The article states:
Exploration permits in Australia are like the old-style permits in the Arctic, says Medcon's Nixon. 'You get a large area and commit yourself to a certain work program. The production lease, what you eventually have to pay, is then defined around what you discover.'
The Australians have learned from Canada. God help them if they ever elect people there who think the way the people in the front benches of this Liberal government think.
I would like to continue with another quote about Australia. This also sounds curiously familiar:
As well, the Australians Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB)-
We have LIRA, the Loreign Investment Review Agency.
-draws just about as much praise from oilmen as Canada's Foreign Investment Review Agency (FIRA) draws criticism.
'The Australian system is a much more workable one from everyone's point of view', says Deacon. 'They don't say everything has to be 50 per cent Australian-owned. They just want 50 per cent ownership once there's production. And once you have reserves, it's easy to get local partners.'
It is easy to get local investors to invest. Of course, that is what we had been doing in Canada for many years. The aim of the National Energy Program to make the oil industry Canadian was already, in fact, happening. It was happening because the Canadian players were becoming involved and were beginning to take over and expand.
People do not realize that we had some of the best technology for oil rig construction situated in western Canada. It was the best of anywhere in the world and we were shipping what was being produced in Canada to fields all over the world. Many people do not know that we developed a new pump in Canada for bringing out of the ground oil which is shipped all over the world. This technology was enabling us to expand the industry.
July 20, 1982

Canada now has the reputation of being unsafe as a place to invest funds. The world no longer trusts Canada. This has been happening over the last two or three years. The government has reneged on agreements with NATO. We have not lived up to our commitments to NATO. More important is the fact that we allowed a government to develop a policy and ram it through Parliament, since we were powerless to stop it, which actually committed outright theft of foreign investment in this country. That policy was the National Energy Program. Once you have had dealings with someone who has not kept his word, you are an absolute fool to return to that person and enter into another agreement. Any lawyer or judge will tell you that. For 30 years Canada was the place to invest. That is no longer the case because confidence and trust have been destroyed. Not only has that trust and confidence been destroyed in our foreign markets, it has been lost in Canada itself.
1 had occasion to walk into the lobby last night where two pages were sitting at a table discussing what would be the best occupation for a young person to take up. All members know these pages.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: You said that last night.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
1 know I said that last night, but it is worth repeating. We know these young pages. They are first year university students who are hopefully looking to what their future in Canada will be. These two pages came to the conclusion that they should enter into business dealings with bankruptcies, because that seems to be where the action presently is. That is a comment on our country. All across the country there are farmers, tradesmen and Canadian developers who have lost confidence in Canada. Canadian businessmen and those hardworking risk takers have lost confidence in Canada as a place to invest.
How do we restore confidence in our country? First, we must withdraw the National Energy Program. We must return to the pre-national energy policy days and restore a positive climate. We must phase out FIRA so that it works along the lines of Australia's review board of being flexible instead of saying to the world: "Foreigners stay out, Yankees stay out, because we do not want your investment." We must remove the taxes that were imposed in the second budget of the Minister of Finance. Those taxes hit every workingman and taxed everything he worked toward.
We must return to the concept that the government does not own everything. Everything should not be taxed. The government must move away from its concept that people cannot donate to charities because the money really belongs to it. Nothing is the government's unless the people want to give. Canadians have not lost confidence in Canada as a country. Canadians have not lost confidence in themselves as individuals. Canadians have not lost confidence in their own individual abilities. Canadians have not lost confidence in their skills, whether they be entrepreneurial skills or working men's skills. Canadians have not lost confidence in themselves to compete on an even footing with any other citizen of the world.
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Canadians know that the land is strong. Do hon. members remember that slogan, "The Land is Strong"? Well, Canadians know the land is strong. Canadians know that we will survive in this country, no matter what the present Liberal government does to the economy. But, hon. friends, Canadians have lost faith in the Prime Minister. Canadians have lost faith in the arrogant Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Canadians have lost faith in the Minister of Finance, who tries to tell us that things are one way when, in fact, they are not, when he dipsy-doos and plays a shell game every time he introduces a budget. Canadians have lost faith in the Minister of State for International Trade who, with his sleazy tactics, does not have the guts to stand up and work out an agreement with the Japanese on car imports but, rather, plays games at the border.
Canadians have lost faith in a government which continually works on brainwashing advertising across the country. Canadians instinctively know that with the God-given resources and talents in this country and our level of education, everything is going for us. But Canadians know that this government is probably the weakest government in the history of Canada and they pray for that group to be gone from this place. I say to all hon. members opposite, on behalf of Canadians across the country who have faith in their country and faith in their land but who have lost all faith in the present government, for God's sake, please do the honourable thing. Resign and go!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are debating the borrowing authority bill which is asking the House of Commons to give authority to the Government of Canada to raise another $11 billion. This is the second time the government has been to the trough and it is doing so because it must make good on the incredible error that it made in the budget of last November. Last November the government said the deficit would be some $10.5 billion. Just two weeks ago, seven months later, we heard that the size of the deficit is some $20 billion.
Let us analyze exactly what the government is requesting. Coming into this fiscal year, there was a carryover of $3.6 billion from the last year. Then, on June 15, the government asked for $6.6 billion worth of borrowing authority. When that is added to the $11 billion that it is requesting now, it amounts to a request for a total of $21.2 billion of borrowing authority, contrasted to the $17.1 billion worth of cash requirement of the government as stated in the budget. That is $4.1 billion more than is needed, a $4.1 billion cushion, or "slush fund", as my friend, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), said. That is a 24 per cent cushion or margin for error that the government says it needs in this borrowing authority. That may seem reasonable in light of the 100 per cent error it made at the time of the last budget, but it is not good enough for the taxpayers of Canada. It is not good enough when we consider the impact of that $20 billion deficit and it is not good enough when we see the impact which loose financial management over the last ten years has had on people in the country today.

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
The figure of $17 billion or $20 billion is huge. It is very hard for anyone to understand the impact or the size of such figures. They are massive and must be put into some form of perspective so that people can get an understanding of exactly what we are discussing here. My colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis), developed some very useful statistics which he put forward in the House a couple of weeks ago. They related to his riding, particularly the City of Belleville, but I have arrived at statistics for my own riding of Etobicoke Centre and the similarity of these statistics is surprising. They give us some idea of just how big $20 billion is.
We all pay municipal taxes in one way or another, whether through rent or as homeowners. Those who are homeowners must write cheques four, five or six times a year for the exact amount of their municipal taxes. Let us look at the $20 billion deficit in relation to municipal taxes. I am just referring to the deficit, not over-all federal government spending, which would be about four and a half times larger. The deficit is equivalent to about $840 per capita, per individual, per man, woman and child in the country today. For the residents of Etobicoke Centre, that works out to about $86.9 million. The total municipal bill in Etobicoke Centre for police and fire protection, for roads, garbage collection, snow removal, public transit and education, amounts to $67.5 million. In other words, our taxes could increase by nearly 30 per cent before the municipal taxes would be equivalent to our share of the federal government deficit. That is the magnitude of the problem which we are letting this government pass on to future generations. The government is spending money so fast now that it is spending the total share of the municipal budget of Etobicoke Centre in seven and a half hours.
Let me give hon. members one more figure. We have seen the government blow about $700 million on Mirabel Airport. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is making a valiant effort to work out that problem right now and he is facing much conflict within his own caucus. That $700 million would pay for Etobicoke Centre's share of all municipal services for over ten years. We would not have to pay another nickel in taxes if that $700 million had been devoted just to Etobicoke Centre. It is easier for all of us to understand the magnitude of the problem when we consider it in terms of our own neighbourhoods. As I say, the Belleville figures are not far off from those of Etobicoke Centre, so I would imagine that there are many communities in Ontario as well as in other parts of Canada which could put the budget deficit in the same perspective and get a better understanding. It is more than equivalent to the municipal taxes all of us are paying across the country.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is asking each Canadian taxpayer to sign a cheque for $2,000 to pay for his mistakes. All Members of Parliament should ask themselves how many of their constituents would be willing today to sign a cheque for $2,000 and send it to the Minister of Finance saying: "Here, Mr. MacEachen, this is to pay for your mistakes and for your shortfall." I do not think many Canadians
today would be prepared to do that. That is a question all Members of Parliament should be asking themselves on behalf of their taxpayers.
It does not stop there. This huge $20 billion deficit has to be financed through borrowing. These deficits are accumulating and have been accumulating year after year since confederation, but not at the alarming rate we have seen in the last few years.
In the early part of the seventies, the budget was just about in balance. There were some deficits, some surpluses. In the last four years, the deficit has averaged $9.5 billion per year. In the current year it will jump to $20 billion. According to an article in Maclean's Magazine, the deficit next year will increase to $22 billion. We have not yet been told those figures. We tried to find that out from the Minister of Finance but he would not tell us what will happen next year. He does not trust us. He does not want us to know the depth of the problem in this country.
Right now the total debt of the country works out to about $5,500 for every man, woman and child, or $14,500 for every taxpayer. As I said earlier, it will jump by another $2,000 after this year to $16,500. The critical element is that we are financing these deficits on an ongoing basis at interest rates between 15 and 20 per cent per annum. That debt accumulates in an alarming way. It doubles every four or five years.
Let us look at last year's deficit of $11.5 billion and this year's deficit of $20 billion and see what will happen to them by 1990 if interest rates stay at the same level they are at today. Those two years alone, nothing else, will build to $116 billion by 1990, almost the size of the total federal government gross debt today.
That is the magnitude of the problem we are dealing with here. That is why we have to do something to get this huge problem down to a size where we can deal with it. We are leaving this problem to our children and grandchildren. We are asking them to pay for the government waste and expenses that Canadians do not want to pay for today. We are mortgaging their future in a major way when the debt is accumulating at rates of interest between 15 and 20 per cent.
Eight years ago $1.00 out of every $9.00 of federal government spending was devoted to payment of interest alone, not repayment of debt but interest alone. Next year one dollar in four of government spending will be devoted to payment of interest on the public debt-no repayment of debt. The government has been asking Canadians to support its irresponsible fiscal policy for ten years.
Economic conditions are getting worse and there is still no effort to turn the matter around. The government is, in effect, asking us to steal from our kids. Each of our children who this year enters the work force will be asked to take on a debt of $14,500 to finance the fiscal mismanagement of the past ten years. That is what we are being asked to do today. That is what we have to change.
July 20, 1982

One of the major goals of this budget is to send a signal to the capital markets today to tell the markets how much of the country's financial resources are to be taken by the federal government. How strongly is the federal government going to compete with other more productive users of capital? That is the $20 billion shock of the budget of June 28.
Government spending this year as a percentage of the overall national income is at 25.3 per cent, a post-war high. This year the government will be taking the largest share of the total economic activity of the country it has taken since the war. That means more taxes for the future. It also means more borrowing in the future.
Let us look at it from the standpoint of the impact of borrowing. In 1980 the net new issues of all securities- federal, municipal, provincial governments, as well as corporations-was $31 billion. In that year the Government of Canada took 36.7 per cent. In 1981 the amount had decreased to $26.8 billion and the government took about 46.5 per cent of that amount. We do not know what the total new issues will be this year, but probably they will be a little lower because of the poor markets we have had. The markets have been devastated by the impact of government policies over the past few years.
However, the Government of Canada will be taking $17 billion of that and it will amount to 60 per cent of the total issues. That is what we mean by crowding out. Borrowers have been crowded out. They have been forced into the banking system as the only source of capital for them.
In 1980-81 the provinces and municipalities were not borrowing a considerable amount of money. In some cases the provincial governments in aggregate were in net surplus. They were not putting much pressure on the markets. This year the problem of crowding out will become compounded because of the increase in borrowing requirements. Therefore the small-business men, home owners, those who want to buy a car, farmers, fishermen and others who need money will have to compete against this massive government borrowing.
When the minister came back from Versailles, he had the audacity to tell us that the big problem in this country today was the huge size of the federal government deficit in the United States. He said if we could only get the United States to deal with its huge deficit problem, we would be better able to solve our problems here. Let us look at the size of the deficit in the United States. On a per capita basis it is about $475. In Canada, as I said a moment ago, it is $780. It is 65 per cent higher in this country than in the United States. That is why we have a problem with interest rates in this country.
Let us look at this in the context of one of the most serious problems we have today, the problem of the severe corporate liquidity squeeze in the country. The Bank of Montreal did a study which it issued last month. It is a very illuminating study because of the generally deteriorating picture across Canada and across industries in the area of corporate liquidity. I want to quote a few statistics. The ratio of interest to pre-tax income in the years 1977 to 1980 has been running at between 20 and 25 per cent a year. In 1981 that figure had increased to 66 per cent. It is bound to go up further this year because of the

continuation of high interest rates and the clearly depressed corporate profit position.
It was announced earlier this year that corporate profits were down between 40 and 50 per cent. Let us put it another way. The coverage of interest by earnings in those earlier years was about five to six times. In 1981 it dropped suddenly to two and one-half times. Various other ratios are quoted which give the same picture.
There is one important figure, critically important today in light of the bankruptcies that have been occurring across the country-the net working capital, the ready cash that keeps a company in business. When there is no working capital, once it has run out, the game is over and the company goes bankrupt. Net working capital in the first half of 1981 actually dropped by $1.7 billion, and that is widely spread across many industries. This report says that some industries are quite vulnerable. It also says: "Should present trends continue, the results will most certainly be disastrous." That is not political rhetoric. That is raw economic analysis based on the facts in the real world today.
For the future the report concludes that the deterioration is accelerating. It does not imply that any real pick-up in activity will be sustained, because of this problem. The response of industry is seen regularly. The clear objective of many companies today is survival. That means cost cutting. That means lay-offs. The struggle for liquidity is really being made on a panic basis. The necessity to preserve cash is essential to the maintenance of business, but the response of the government in the face of this problem is business as usual. "We increased our spending last year by 20 per cent; let's increase our spending this year by another 20 per cent." For two years running spending will increase by 20 per cent.
As 1 said before, Maclean's had told us that the budget deficit is forecast by some people in the Department of Finance to be another $3 billion. That means we will have continuing pressure on interest rates. It means that people who need to raise money for new cars, homes, rolling over mortgages or for the maintenance of small businesses will be under severe pressure when they have to raise money.
We in the Progressive Conservative Party have been very conscious of this sharp deterioration in the economy. We warned of it last September, and we are very conscious of the impact of the huge $20 billion deficit on the very weak position of Canadian industry today. We have continuously been proposing clear alternatives to the measures proposed by the Liberals and New Democrats in order to ease this situation. First, we have said there must be restraint in government spending. We must have a board program to cut discretionary spending by up to 10 per cent. The prime focus of this type of spending cut would be in areas such as government advertising, which clearly is not essential; in rental costs and professional and consulting fees; and in general materials rented by government departments across the board. This has to be done

Supplementary Borrowing Authority
in an equitable way. Let us not be fooled by the questions hon. members opposite put to us. They say, "Where would you cut?" Cuts cannot be made in one particular area or another; there has to be a broad attack on discretionary spending across the board. Back in 1979 we showed that it can be done. We have shown that the Conservative Party, with a commitment, an understanding of the problem and the necessary management skills, can do it. At that time we kept government spending 2.5 percentage points below the rate of growth in the national income.
The second point is that we could reduce the pressure on the Canadian dollar by changing the policies which have caused that pressure. My colleague, the hon. member for Athabasca, referred to the National Energy Program and clearly set out in his speech that that program is one of those policies which has caused that pressure on the Canadian dollar. The Foreign Investment Review Agency has policies which are scaring money away from the country. My colleague discussed that as well. It is clear to all Canadians that downward pressure on the Canadian dollar is leading to upward pressure on interest rates. High interest rates only aggravate the tremendous corporate liquidity problem we have today. That is causing the lay-offs which are swelling the unemployment ranks in the country today.
The third objective should be to create a more favourable investment climate by reversing those parts of the November budget which have undermined the investment climate in the country and have dulled the investment intentions of Canadian business.
All these policy initiatives would lead to a reduction in the deficit, a reduction in interest rates and an easing of our economic problems. The over-all result would be a reduction in the federal government deficit. Let me make it quite clear that the federal government deficit will not be cut just by cutting spending alone. It will be reduced only if we get economic activity going and if we bring about a reduction in interest rates.
The three-point program I have just outlined would go far in achieving the objectives of growth and lower interest rates, but cost cutting is also a very important element in sending a signal to the private sector that Canadians can understand. Canadians should expect that the government means business about controlling its spending and reducing the deficit. That signal has never come. The minister says that the Government of Canada will limit the growth in its spending below the growth in the economy. That is a cruel joke because government spending, two years running now, has been increasing 20 per cent per annum. But then the minister goes on and bleats about all the expenditures which are totally outside his control. He says he can do nothing about them because they are statutory or they are contractual. The minister has a point there, but those of us who have families and have to control our family expenses and those of us who have small businesses or large businesses and have to control our business expenses all have contractual expenses such as rent and interest. We
also have to eat, but if our over-all spending increases faster than we can afford, we cut back.
Let us look at the basis on which the government would judge itself. Let us look just at discretionary programs, the programs I said we would have to cut, in terms of spending, by 10 per cent. What has happened? The amounts spent on those programs have increased at a rate 2.5 percentage points faster than the rate of growth in the economy this year. So much for what the government says is its prime yardstick for judging whether it is restraining itself. That restraint is just not there.
Hon. members may wonder why I have been so concerned about government spending. Let me put it in the most simple terms I can. Government spending leads to higher taxes, higher taxes lead to more spending, and so on. It is a vicious circle. Just to illustrate my point, let us look back at the 1980, 1981 and 1982 budgets. They are perfect textbook illustrations. The 1980 budget imposed higher taxes through energy taxes. We found out that tax revenues were expected to increase 31 per cent one year and 50 per cent over a two-year period. However, that higher tax revenue led to slackness in control of government spending. As I said a minute ago, we have seen that government spending increased 20 per cent one year and then 20 per cent the next year.
What happened in last November's budget? One does not need to be a genius to figure it out. The government came to the trough and said: "We have to increases taxes $1.4 billion," and it did so under the guise of tax reform. What do we have as a result of the increased spending in the June budget? We have a $1.3 billion increase in spending under the guise of deindexation.
The tragic part of this $2.7 billion increase in taxes is that we are in a serious recession. This is the first time we have had taxes increased by this magnitude in a recession since the 1930s. There is no economic theory which calls for increasing taxes in the middle of a serious recession. I do not believe the goals of Canadians to generate economic growth, to reduce unemployment and to preserve our economic freedoms are met by increasing taxes in a recession. We have to make a fresh start by reducing government spending if we are to get off this vicious circle and meet the objectives I am sure all Canadians have.
Let me make one other thing clear. I say in all seriousness that the job of the Minister of Finance is to protect the fiscal integrity of the Government of Canada and to manage the nation's finances in a prudent and proper way. The Minister of Finance has failed in relation to those objectives. He has failed in his responsibilities. Inflation is running at 11 per cent to 12 per cent per annum. The value of the Canadian dollar dropped from 87 cents at the time the minister took over his job to 77 cents and then around 76 cents a few weeks ago. It is now bubbling along at about 79 cents. The human toll of this 10.9 per cent unemployment rate, representing 1.3 million unemployed, says it all. It shows where the minister has failed. All of these figures represent a devastating condemnation of the minister's performance on the job.
July 20, 1982

Let us consider what might happen next year, Mr. Speaker. We have no projections. The Minister of Finance has said that he cannot give us projections because he does not know what is going to happen and he does not trust his figures. At the same time he has enough contempt for this Parliament to come here and ask us to authorize $11 billion more borrowing to carry over to the next fiscal year when he has not even given us projections for that fiscal year.
Some of us have done the calculations, Mr. Speaker. Some of us have some understanding of what the figures for next year might be. We believe that the Maclean's magazine figure of $22 billion is correct and it is for that reason that we are resisting the government's request for another $11 billion borrowing authority.
This uncertainty in the future is the cause for real concern in business in Canada. Business fears that the $22 billion deficit figure for next year will be low and that the pressures on the market, on interest rates, for financing businesses and households, rollovers on mortgages, new cars and other goods that need a bank loan, will be even greater. Confidence is bound to remain low if people do not trust the government's ability to see ahead into next year.
Canadians want to hear the truth today. They want to know how serious the outlook is in the minister's view. He must tell Canadians what that truth is. It may be his last chance to tell the truth, Mr. Speaker.
Most of all, Canadians want the government to live within its means and not to ask the rest of the country to make sacrifices. From the June 28 budget we see that the country is in a real bind. The government wants all Canadians to move to the 6 per cent world of recovery, but at the same time it wants to stay in its dream world of 20 per cent spending increases. While the rest of the country has to suffer with a 6 per cent increase, the government is going to increase its net debt by a full 18 per cent.
The Minister of Transport and others in the government have expressed some doubts about whether Canadians will move to the 6 per cent world. This is why Canadians are reluctant, Mr. Speaker, because they do not feel they are being treated fairly. They do not believe the government is committed to deal with the problems of the country. It is either that or the government does not have the intelligence or the confidence in Canadians to understand that they are not treating them equitably, with a fair hand. That is the problem we are facing today.
I want to comment briefly on the amendment moved by my leader yesterday, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would prefer to defer the question until I finish my remarks. After that I would be prepared to accept a question.
The first amendment we offered was to decline second reading of this bill. There is a well established principle that Parliament only provides sufficient borrowing authority to a government to allow it to finance its operations within the current fiscal year. It is quite clear from the figures in the bill and from the statement by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) in response to my question yesterday that the government has every intention of this borrowing authority spilling over into 1983-84.
This is all the more reprehensible because the government has not given us any projections about what will happen in 1983-84. If things are too uncertain for it to predict what is going to happen in 1983-84, then it is too uncertain for us to give it the carte blanche freedom to go on spending money like a drunken sailor. It is for that reason that we feel the government should withdraw this bill and offer something that will allow it to live within its means. This bill is clearly objectionable. I believe that amendment must be and will be supported by other members of the House.
The second part of the amendment put forward by my leader yesterday was to the effect that after this bill before us is withdrawn and replaced, we expect the government to reduce its borrowing requirement in view of what we have said about the level of increase in government spending. It is clear that the impact of this borrowing will lead to an increase in interest rates. Canadians do not need an increase in interest rates, Mr. Speaker. It is absolutely essential that the government embark on a program to cut its spending to reduce its safety cushion, the margin for error, the slush fund of that $4 billion requested in this bill. It is for that reason that we believe that, together with a reduction of some $2 billion in cash balances, the borrowing authority can be cut back to $5 billion through these three steps.
It is also very clear that the budget was a short-term response to our immediate economic and political problems. It is not a long-term solution. It is not part of any long-term plan. I believe a long-term plan will have to be presented to the House some time in the fall. Perhaps the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) will give us an indication of that when he speaks.
At that time the government will give its projections for the next fiscal year and we hope it will get back to giving projections on a five-year plan as in previous budgets. At that time we should be asked to give the full borrowing authority that will carry the government through, based on those projections. In the meantime, the House should be asked only to provide borrowing authority until the end of November or possibly the end of December. The figure of $5 billion should be more than sufficient to meet those requirements.
The second amendment regarding future borrowing authority would provide greater protection for taxpayers. Currently there is no over-all limit on borrowings by Crown corporations and no limitation on the total amount of guarantees that the

government can give out in loans under the enterprise development program, for Canadair or for financial rescue operations such as Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson. For most Crown corporations the only authority necessary is the approval of the Minister of Finance.
Let us consider the loophole in the borrowing authority, Mr. Speaker. Many of the large Crown corporations, such as the EDC, Petro-Canada, Eldorado or the Federal Business Development Bank, can borrow directly from the government or go to the public market. If the government falls short in its estimate of what the deficit will be, then the minister will be under pressure not to come back to the Flouse but to push some of the Crown corporations into the open market and free borrowing room for the Government of Canada directly. Whatever happens, the net result is that the exposure of the taxpayer will be increased and Parliament will have lost control of the over-all borrowing by the government or of borrowing indirectly through Crown corporations.
Let us consider another possibility. Many companies are under severe financial pressure today. I discussed that matter earlier in my speech. Some of these will come to the government directly for help and some have done so already. We must have more control over this area, Mr. Speaker. The amendment asks for three things on this score: We want an over-all limitation on the amount of borrowing by Crown corporations-so-called off balance sheet borrowing; we want an over-all limitation on the total amount of government guarantees of loans; we want an annual report setting out in one place all the information on this type of financing which is supported by the government; or, to be more precise, which represents an indirect call on the resources of the taxpayer.
We do not know today what the total amount of Crown corporation borrowing is and we do not know what the over-all amount of government guarantees is. We feel that it is essential that taxpayers and voters have this information. We do not know either, in these hard times, how many government guarantees will be called on. We have had two examples in the last six or seven months, Massey-Ferguson and Consolidated Computer Corporation, involving an aggregate amount of around $350 million.
We are making these I believe very responsible requests because we believe this type of disclosure and control is necessary. I do not believe there is one taxpayer in the country who would not give us support. I call on members opposite to discuss these proposals with the Minister of Finance and encourage and pressure him to allow an amendment or, if not an amendment, a form of legislation which will provide this protection to the taxpayer.
I serve notice on members opposite and the three ministers present that this is not a frivolous request designed to waste the time of the House. It is a very serious and I believe very reasonable request for a much tighter degree of control over government financing. I also say to the ministers opposite that with that type of control they will be in a much stronger
position to resist the pressures which are bound to be applied to them in the months and years ahead.
The evidence is very clear, Mr. Speaker; this government must reduce the borrowing requirement. It does not need all the money it has requested. The government has hidden from Members of Parliament the complete picture of its over-all requirements and it has made no attempt to control spending. The already severe liquidity crisis which all corporations are experiencing is being added to enormously by pressures from the increased government borrowing, and it is also increasing the unemployment problem in the country today. The crowding out of private sector borrowers and the increase in interest rates due to competition from the government is intense. Finally, the forecast increase in spending is bound to lead to higher taxes as we get more and more engrossed in that vicious circle I referred to earlier.
The government must give serious consideration to the alternative policies we have put forward to ease this liquidity crisis and the pressure on interest rates. The government must amend the bill to remove those loopholes which allow unlimited borrowing by Crown corporations and unlimited guarantees by the government. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I feel this bill must be opposed.

I am a little puzzled about one statement he made, that the Canadian deficit is about 65 per cent higher than the U.S. deficit on a per capita basis. 1 hope he is comparing the same years because, do not forget, the American fiscal year is October to September and ours is April to March.
What figures is the hon. member using? OECD uses a figure of about $150 billion; some of the figures coming out now in the U.S. show the deficit this year could be $125 billion, and up to $170 billion or $180 billion next year. The figures I get seem to indicate that the deficits of each country are very close to each other on a per capita basis.

Mr. Speaker, in view of some of the speeches we heard yesterday and today in

this debate, 1 think it is important to remember that we are dealing with a borrowing bill, not with a budget and specifically not with the deficit. It is money that government needs to meet its commitments for pensions, family allowances and other programs which hon. members feel are important to the country. In due course I will be talking about why such a deficit exists at the present time, but the distinction must clearly be made between the excellent budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has presented and the question of the deficit, which results not only from what has happened to our economy but also what has happened to the economies of the United States and other countries of the free world.
Without question we are confronted today with a serious recession both here and in the U.S. Even in West Germany, a country which ever since its recovery after World War II has seemed to be immune to unemployment, the recession has brought a higher level of unemployment than has been experienced in North America.
Having said that we are dealing with a borrowing bill, 1 want to start by saying a word about the speech made in this debate by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) yesterday.
