Of course, there are areas in which a prudent government would not venture to begin with, let alone maintain itself in that position. Those decisions are pretty difficult ones but some of them could be made. I will give the minister an example of one which could be taken right now. It will save millions and millions of dollars of public money that would unnecessarily be committed to a program that, in terms of the efficiency of the delivery of services of the particular department, could mean great savings, if one could measure efficiency in the public sector. I have in mind the announcement made July 13, 1982, of the decentralization of the incomes security program by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
It is very interesting to note that in the decentralization program is the move of the existing large incomes security Ontario regional office located in Toronto to four places, Peterborough, Chatham and Timmins, with one part remaining in Toronto. Also the Canada Pension Plan operation for the processing of Ontario benefits will be dispersed from the national capital area to those same four regional offices, including Toronto. Also, the incomes security regional office for Nova Scotia, which is in Halifax, is going to be relocated to Sydney, Nova Scotia.
It is interesting that when that announcement is made there is no corresponding statement about what it is going to cost. I wager I am low when I suggest that that move involving moving expenses of families, the acquisition of land, the development of buildings and equipment, the purchase of equipment, etc, etc, ad nauseam, will cost $75 million. If it does not, I will apologize to this House. There is one suggestion.
When we were in office, we looked at the decentralization program. The hon. member says I am interested in it. Of course I am. I have always said that if it is rational to have bits and pieces of departments and agencies in the regions, that is an excuse for a regional development program. When I was minister of national revenue, in only one case did I not recommend against the decentralization program of a department, because it made sense to bring the components of that department out into the country. However, there were 19 others we looked at which we stopped. It would have involved millions and millions in government expenditures. Some finality had to be given. There was a demand upon the public purse which was not as great as it is today.
That the government should continue that program in the face of a $20 billion deficit borders on the immoral. If the minister wants to know where to begin a tremendous savings programs, that is the place. He asked for a beginning. There is
July 20, 1982

one. It could save the country a great deal of money, not just in raw dollars but in terms of loss of efficiency.
Members of Parliament should ask their colleagues in cabinet to show them the cabinet documents that exist with respect to the advice from the public service as to the inefficacy in terms of administration and delivery of services as well by the decentralization program. If my friends opposite, on seeing those documents, believe that is the way to spend our money, I would suggest that their judgment is pretty far gone. My suggestion to the government is to stop that silliness. There are other priorities in the country that are much more important and there could be savings of a tremendous amount of public money.
There is a second area I want the government to look at. It is important that we look at some of the decisions made by certain agencies. 1 hope that members opposite understand the tremendous losses of CMHC and thereby the public of Canada with respect to some projects. I invite my friends opposite to look at this one. CMHC lost over $100 million on the 1981 property sales it made. It had a sizeable inventory of housing units acquired as a result of defaults and abandonments. It sold off a significant amount of property at far below the market value. As I said, the losses for 1980 are estimated at $100 million. The principal beneficiaries of those sales have not been the taxpayers of Canada. They have been the developers and housing speculators. I will give two examples.
In September, 1980, 1,130 CMHC housing units in the Outaouais area of west Quebec, valued at $45,000 per unit, were sold to a group of businessmen for $7,079 per unit. Consider whether it might have been more prudent to have kept those on inventory.
In early 1981, Steveston Enterprises of Vancouver paid $18,500 per unit for 42 London, Ontario townhouses with market values of $23,300 to $59,000. They paid $14,700 per unit for 50 Oshawa, Ontario, townhouses valued at $30,000 to $33,000 per unit. The average loss on the sale in London, Ontario, was $20,000 per unit. The average loss on the sale in Oshawa was $25,000 per unit. Think of it. CMHC did not have to sell those properties. However, as a result of making that so-called business decision there was that loss not only of the units into the hands of speculators but loss to the taxpayers of Canada. Somewhere in the $20 billion deficit must be shown those figures. I could go on. Some of the things that have happened are almost unbelievable.
Can you imagine the Canadian National Railways spending $64,244 to purchase advertising space to wish its competitor, CPR, a happy birthday? Can you imagine that kind of expenditure by a Crown corporation, a public agency? Can you imagine paying two chefs $110,000 in 1981 for cooking lessons? Bruno Gerussi and Madame Benoit were given six-week television contracts worth $110,000 to promote metric cooking.
I want members to imagine the thinking which goes into that kind of a decision. Just imagine it. Then we in this House are asked to approve of a bill authorizing the borrowing of an amount which the minister admits is far more than he needs. It
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
is no wonder that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) moved the following amendment in the House yesterday:
-this House holds the opinion that the granting of an authority for the borrowing of a sum greater than that amount which is required to meet the government's needs to the end of the current fiscal year is objectionable in principle and this House therefore declines to give second reading to Bill C-125, An Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority.
What is implicit in that amendment by the Leader of the Opposition is whether this government, which has demonstrated year after year its failure internally to put some harness on expenses and on the letting of public contracts and to provide some judgment with respect to that matter, which is apparent to the Canadian public, ought to be trusted with more money than it absolutely needs.
The Secretary of State discussed what a banker would ask a person wishing to borrow money from his bank. A banker asks what assets a person has. Certainly the firm called Canada is rich in assets; no one will argue about that. That is in every high school essay that was ever written. It is also in every ministerial speech ever given. The banker would ask about the future potential prospects of the business enterprise called Canada. I would like to believe what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said. I have not seen much of it in the latter part of the twentieth century, but he said that the twentieth century belongs to Canada.
Most Canadians are beginning to think that the twentieth century belongs to our creditors, and that is one of the problems, but I would like to believe that in the long term there is a future because the people of Canada always have the ability to change the government. Then the banker would ask about security. No one would argue that Canada cannot provide security, but there is not a member of the House of Commons who does not know of a business which has had great assets, great potential and a great level of security but which, as a result of poor management, poor policies and bad investments, has gone down the drain.
The minister did not mention one other question that banker would ask the person coming in and looking for a line of credit: What about one's attitude? What is the attitude of the business enterprise called Canada and its board of directors toward proper management? I have some documents about bad management, and I have seen others, which would make the hair of the hon. member from Middlesex turn greyer than it is. I have mentioned some examples of bad management.
We are in a period of restraint which is so bad that the government is attacking the pensions of ordinary senior citizens and reducing indexation by 6 per cent. It is so bad that the government is going to breach the contract it made with federal public servants with respect to recognizing increases in the cost of living. In this situation can hon. members imagine that an agency of the government, the National Capital Commission, in November of 1981 decided to change the colour of its trucks from green, black and white to brown and beige-a matter of tremendous public importance!-at a cost of $1.4 million?

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
1 am hearing from the senior citizens who were attacked by the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). They now feel a sense of insecurity because increases in their incomes are being limited to 6 per cent. They are asking who is trying to kid whom. What those people are paying for-and they know it-is year upon year of inefficiency and year upon year of wrongheadedness. They are now paying the piper for the tune called a long time ago, which was wrong. These people will remember. They remembered the "six-buck boys" when Walter Harris was minister of finance. That is all he could give for old age security. Pensioners today will remember the "six per cent boys and girls" when the next election is called, because this government has removed from the senior citizens of this country that sense of security which was very important to them and which, by the way, was one of the bottom lines of the great humanists in the Liberal Party of Canada.
There are other victims of the foolishness of the government, which asks other people to pay the price of its stupidity. The government asks this of people who are not protected and who no longer are in the work force. I want to put their case here today in the context of a bill in which this government asks for more money than it needs to finance the foolishness of the past. That is exactly what this bill requires. I think it is absolutely wrong, in the context of the waste and extravagance which has gone on, for the Minister of Finance to announce on budget night that the government will finally breach an agreement made many years ago with the federal public service of Canada. That agreement was with respect to the pensions of public servants. By agreement over a long period of time, those pensions were to reflect the cost of living. Public servants made contributions in relation to that agreement. The federal government also made contributions over the years pursuant to that contract.
I think what is happening now is wrong, and I want members of this House of Commons to consider what is happening. I refer particularly to members who represent public servants, including the Secretary of State. I refer also to members from the National Capital Commission area on both sides of the Ottawa River who represent public servants. I hope they are successful in ensuring that the bill-it has to be a bill-never sees the light of day, because it is wrong.
1 want to put some things on the record because I want members of this House to understand how wrong it is. Not only are retired public servants to be subject to the reduced indexing of their old age security payments and of their income tax exemptions; they are, if the budget proposal is not withdrawn, to have payments out of the several superannuation accounts to which they and the government as their employer have contributed treated as though they were subject to appropriation at the whim of the government rather than administered in accordance with the terms established by Parliament and communicated to public servants before they retired. All of the government's indexing proposals, with the sole exception of the indexing of public service pensions, relate to the government's budgetary revenue and expenditure accounts. The limitation on the indexing of public servants'
pensions, however, is the only proposal which will affect a trust or pension account held by the government for the benefit of a specified group of citizens. That was money committed by public servants through deductions for that indexing provision and money committed by the government, impressed with a trust. That is the way that should be regarded.
The understanding which retired public servants have of their pension entitlements in so far as indexing is concerned is summed up in a booklet from the Treasury Board entitled "Your Superannuation Plan, 1974 Edition," and I will quote from that as follows:
There is no means test and all in receipt of pensions, whether former employees or their widows and dependants, benefit from the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act's provisions. In any year where there is an increase in the cost of living, pensions will be increased in an amount directly related to the increase in the Consumer Price Index, without limit. The percentage increase payable each January represents the increase of the average of the Consumer Price Index for the twelve-month period ending on the preceding September over that for the twelve-month period of the previous year.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) put it even more simply about a year ago when he said that the federal government remained dedicated to the principle that public service pensions are to be protected from inflation. But there goes the commitment of the government, blasted away by the budget of June 28.
On the basis of guarantees made over the years, pensioners planned their retirement and entered into all the commitments associated therewith. We believe that they had every reason to count that their expectations would be met. Even in the depression the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, while reducing salaries of public servants by 10 per cent and withholding all annual increases, held the existing pension arrangements in respect of retired employees inviolate.
Those who would cheer this proposal of the government ought to remember that it has been recognized for years that pension rights accumulated during the period of employment form part of the total compensation package earned by the employee. Time and time again the President of the Treasury Board has said that this is deferred wages, that it is earned income. Now, because it is short of funds, the government decides to breach an agreement.
I have talked to people who were involved in the early days of the negotiations and asked them what the attitude was at that time. Mr. Leslie Barnes, during the time he was President of PIPS and afterwards when he was executive director, was present during the negotiations when Arnold Heeney was involved in the public service. At that time the Public Service Employment Act was being amended. The staff associations wanted pensions to be a bargainable issue but Mr. Heeney, quite properly, pointed out that was a difficult thing to do because it was difficult to bargain certain things that were fixed by statute. A consensus was arrived at.
A gentleman's agreement was reached to the effect that, while pensions as such would not be bargainable, the right to
July 20, 1982

them would be enshrined. That meant that any amendment to a pension scheme would be done by mutual consent, not unilaterally. This recent action was a unilateral move on the part of the government. Some people think that this is not such a terrible thing, that the public service will go to a 6 per cent pay increase and, as pensions reflect income, they will be increased as well. Any one who has thought about the matter knows that any amount lost to a public servant as a result of a change in indexing is lost forever. It will never be recovered. The contribution is really the premium for an insurance scheme. If inflation came down to zero and there was no indexing of pensions, the 1 per cent contribution of the public servant would continue to be paid and the 1 per cent contributed by the government would continue to be paid. The public servant would receive no benefit, yet his contribution would continue.
The government must think about what it intended. Unlike members of the active work force, pensioners have no way of recovering this loss in the future. They cannot bargain, so they must look to Parliament. They can look to the government, with despair, but they must look to Parliament to be fair and reasonable and keep agreements that have been made.
The typical public servant who retired on pension in the last financial year, after about 25 years' service, received a pension of about $8,000 per annum. If the government's proposals are implemented, that will reduce the real value of such a pension to about $7,200 for the rest of the pensioner's life. One third of all those who retired during the same period on pensions of $5,500 or less will suffer a permanent 10 per cent cut while the surviving spouse's meagre pension of about $2,000 will shrink in real terms to $1,800.
More than money is involved, Mr. Speaker; there is a question of morality. I suppose the government has a legal right to act fraudulently. Some people say that Parliament can turn a woman into a man and a man into a woman if it is necessary; if it cannot do that, it can come close to it. Parliament can do all kinds of things, some that are legal but also some that are immoral.
I believe this will be an immoral act, Mr. Speaker. I believe also that this particular aspect should be fought for what it is-a fraud on the thousands and thousands of people in the Public Service of Canada who made a contribution for that extra benefit, in good faith.
The President of the Treasury Board told me in the House and at the miscellaneous estimates committee that the government was going to deal with this question in the total consideration of pensions and that it did not intend to deal with it in isolation. Now it has dealt with it in isolation, Mr. Speaker. There is no way that any right thinking member of this House can support this kind of double dealing, shot in the dark, stab in the back approach to the employees of the government.
The people who are now asking serving public servants to accept a decrease in their income of 6 and 5 per cent know that they are to be involved in a two-year program. The government said so, if it can be believed. People are suspicious about other things but they know that. They also know that they belong to bargaining units which can bargain at the appropriate time. I
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
believe that it is important that the government and its supporters consider the difference between its serving public servants and those who are retired.
The calls that I have received were not with respect to the 6 and 5 per cent, Mr. Speaker. People are not happy with that any more than I am happy with Bill C-124, but there is a latent anger in the public service about the pension system to which they have contributed and about which a solemn undertaking was given by the government of the day and repeated by successive governments. Public servants and their families know that throughout the years an abatement was reflected in salary negotiations because of a contribution made to the total compensation package paid to public servants, including the pension.
I ask the government to reconsider its position because I think this is important. If it needs any help I can supply it. I have here a letter from the wife of a retired public servant who lives on Evergreen Drive in the city of Nepean. This is what she writes to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen):
I was shocked to hear in your Budget speech on Monday evening that you are putting a ceiling on indexing the public servants' superannuation for two years.
I feel that this action would be a serious breach of contract with public service pensioners. Indexing pensions to inflation has already been paid for jointly by the employee and employer, by mutual agreement. To use these funds for other purposes would be dishonest in the extreme.
I trust that you will reconsider this proposal.
Another retired public servant from Richmond, Ontario wrote to the Minister of Finance, and this is what he said:
The general reason is that this government for the past several years has ignored economic issues, with the sole exception of the NEP, and is now up to its eyes in debt. Instead it has sloganeered on national unity, Constitution, bills of rights, Quebec separation etc. It hoped that the U.S. would recover from its recession and bring Canada up with it. Tough luck for us that it has not.
The specific reason pensioners are to be penalized is because they are as a group weak, inarticulate and not politically active. They tend to be loyal and maybe a little old fashioned, and are now being punished for being so. Their votes can be bought just before the next election by raising the index a little. And they will be grateful.
The letter concludes this way:
Further, pensioners do not have a Chamber of Commerce, a John Bulloch or a professional association to speak for them. It is significant that the only pensioners who have not been caused to take a pension loss are the veterans, who have the Canadian Legion to defend their interest.
Referring to the Minister of Finance it says:
You know as well as I that inflation will be closer to 20 per cent than 6 per cent in the next year. Meanwhile, pensioners will still have to pay proportionately more of their income to dentists ($68 for a '/: hour) and extra billing surgeons ($220 for a % hour) than the general population, in addition to basic necessities. And that on a lower income and higher taxes.
In conclusion, referring to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), he says:
Mr. Taylor was correct when he said the government's actions were "legally right but not morally right".
I ask every member of the House to consider that particular position. Mr. Speaker, members ask where we can save money. Everyone knows where we can save money. The work of the
19524

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
committee dealing with parliamentary reform is to provide within this Parliament ways in which members can appropriately scrutinize government programs. It is not there to tear out the guts of programs necessary for the people of Canada, but surely there is no one in the House, given the litany I just began to recite, because it goes on for page after page of examples of foolishness, stupidity and extravagance, who could ever trust this government with the extra money over and above what the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) says is needed. Therefore, I support the motion of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I do not believe any right thinking member of this House could do anything but say to this government: get your own act together, look after your own people properly, and do not blame your foolishness on others. Do not ask of Canadians that which you do not need, and do not do to Canadians what you promised you would not do.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise today to participate in the debate on Bill C-125, the supplementary borrowing authority, 1982-83, with which once again the government has to come before Parliament-this time rather unexpectedly-to
ask for authority to borrow such a vast amount of money to see us through the remainder of this particular fiscal year and well into the next. I have had the opportunity to participate in a number of these debates in this, the Thirty-second Parliament, and I remember that in its first borrowing authority bill the government asked permission to borrow $12 billion. A number of months later a second request to borrow $14 billion came along, and then just a few weeks ago the government again came to Parliament feeling that it needed $6.6 billion. That request received Royal Assent on June 17, 1982, and four weeks later the government is back asking permission to borrow $11 billion to see us through the remainder of the year. In one session, so far, the government has asked to borrow $43.6 billion. What has been the result? Presumably that money has resulted in a variety of government programs serving the people of Canada well, providing opportunities for Canadians to be productive, and meet their obligations to their friends, families and the economy generally. However, when we review the facts, we find that quite a different picture emerges.
I do not have to remind members of the House that today we are experiencing in Canada an unemployment situation which has not been duplicated since the hungry thirties. Nearly two million Canadians find themselves in a state of forced idleness. People who normally have led productive lives and contributed to the development of the Canadian economy all their lives, now find themselves for the first time in a situation where they are no longer able to provide as they would like for themselves, their families and their country. We are experiencing a situation in which the Auditor General himself, Kenneth Dye, is quoted as saying, "The country is close to being on its economic knees." That is the Auditor General of Canada, a man responsible for overseeing the fiscal affairs of government and a man who presumably has to inform Canadians as to how well the government is doing. This man, who is in a very serious position and knows full well that his words are going to be considered very seriously by every Canadian, says that the country is close to being on its economic knees. The former auditor general, Mr. James Mac-donell, made a similar comment recently when he said, "We are going down the bloody drain if we don't do something about it." He actually said that, the former auditor general of this country, that we are going down the bloody drain. I suppose that means one thing to one person and something quite different to another. Being "on its economic knees" might be interpreted in different ways by different people, but one thing that everyone agrees on is that our economy is in an economic crisis. It would not be difficult to add that it is in a social crisis as well.
Earlier today one of my colleagues raised in the House the matter of a social phenomenon which is taking on unprecedented dimensions, that of violence to women in our society.
July 20, 1982

While one might have difficulty in making the direct connection between that and our economic crisis, one would have no difficulty in recognizing some relationship between those two phenomena. Of course, we could add to that the rising incidence of child abuse, wife battering, drug and alcohol abuse, and a long litany of other social problems which indeed have a very direct relationship to our economic recession, or depression as more and more people are calling it.
The $43.6 billion which the government has asked this Parliament to provide for its economic mismanagement has resulted not only in two million people being unemployed or in a state of forced idleness but also in the economy being generally on the ropes. It has resulted also in such things as a 60 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies in the first six months of this year compared to the first six months of last year, and last year was bad enough.
Mir. Miller: Last year was terrible.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Last year was terrible, as my colleague has just indicated. Last year was a very bad year for those in the food producing industries. Business bankruptcies generally are up 37 per cent in the first six months of 1982 compared with the same period in 1981. That is only the tip of the iceberg, Mr. Speaker. When we speak of business bankruptcies, we do not mention the receivership proceedings that are in place. It is estimated that between three and five times the number of bankruptcies occur in the receivership form. Of course, that does not touch those thousands of small businesses and medium-sized businesses that are simply closing their doors nor their owners who are walking away from their hopes and their dreams. By the end of this year, I suspect that if the figures could be obtained, we would find that in excess of 20,000 businesses have folded as a result of the economic crisis which this government has perpetuated. Indeed, I think we have to recognize that there is an unholy alliance between the Progressive Conservative and the Liberal parties of Canada. When one considers that we are dealing with the federal government, one must note that we are also dealing with the mismanagement that has happened in a variety of provincial jurisdictions. It is not surprising that those provincial jurisdictions are almost exclusively Tory in terms of their leadership.
The situation with respect to the economic capacity of this country at the moment is very serious. We have a 69 per cent operating capacity in our manufacturing productive sector, which is resulting in shutdowns, cutbacks, freezes, lay-offs, threats of lay-off and threats of closure. When you walk through the shops of Canada, you find they are largely empty. People do not have the purchasing power that they had. Those who are fortunate to have jobs today or those who have a few dollars in their savings account are not going to risk spending that money with the uncertainty that prevails across this fine land today. With no one buying goods or services, the government came in with a new budget in June saying, "We have an answer. The reason our factories are not at full capacity and our shops are not producing as they should is that people are not buying the goods and services as they did in the past." The
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
government told us it had the answer. The government said, "We are going to raise taxes across the board." But that measure will take more of the purchasing power out of the hands of Canadians. The government said, "Listen, we want to focus in on certain groups. The senior citizens are a good group. Let us reduce the benefits going to senior citizens. That will help the economy surely." Then the government looked at increasing energy costs. The government's increasing the costs of energy will improve the situation. The government said, "We will jack up the energy costs this year by 20 per cent and by 31 per cent next year." The government said that it will keep interest rates high so that no one will be encouraged to expand his plant, factory, shop or build a home.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Eighteen cents a gallon turned out to be a buck.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Those are the kinds of solutions, if you can believe it, Mr. Speaker, that this government has brought to Canadians, saying, "Here is the way to get out of our economic recession or the beginning of a serious depression." What a way, raising taxes, hitting senior citizens, jacking up interest rates and energy costs. That logic escapes me.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That logic is illogical.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
As my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain suggests, rather than logic there is a certain amount of illogic involved in the suggestion that this is the way to get us out of our economic malaise.
It is the human suffering, the human tragedy, the pessimism, the gloom and doom, and the down and out syndrome that prevails now in all parts of Canada as a result of improper policies having been introduced by this government in difficult times. That is the real price this country is paying today. People have lost faith and they have lost trust in this government.
Let us look at a few facts, Mr. Speaker. Often when government members stand up in their places and present us with the picture as they see it, it is easy to manufacture facts. It is easy to manufacture statistics or slant statistics in a certain way or to create a certain impression by leaving out certain numbers in a statistical review. Let us be very straightforward and let us keep the numbers to a minimum.
Let us review what has happened in the last little while. Canada's accumulated debt is now over $108 billion. That, in more personal terms, is $4,400 for every man, woman and child in the country, or over $10,000 for every person who is lucky enough to be employed in this country today. That debt will cost Canadians $17.7 billion to service this year. That is over 25 per cent of the projected revenues for this year, from 22 per cent last year and from 19 per cent the year before. Thirty years ago it was only 9.7 per cent. This government is putting us further and further into an economic mess.
The government's expenses rose by $400 million due to increases in the cost of UIC alone. However, the burden on taxpayers is much greater. Premiums on employees and employers account for 80 per cent of UIC financing. With

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
high unemployment UIC will accumulate a deficit of at least $2.2 billion this year. This means premiums for UIC will have to be raised this fall between 50 per cent and 100 per cent. That is the kind of program which this government appears to be interested in perpetuating, that of a deficit and, of all things, in the unemployment insurance fund.
One could go on and on. Projects for income from corporate taxes have fallen from $2.75 billion in the November to June period. The revenue expected from federal sales taxes has fallen $820 million in the last seven months because the economy has slowed down to such an extent. What makes matters worse is that the imaginative program of the 6 per cent world, to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) refers repeatedly and the fact that he feels the solution to our problems is to restrict wages and salaries to federal employees, will take $500 million per year out of the economy of the national capital alone. What does that say to the small business people in the national capital of Canada, that $900 million will be taken out annually from their pockets as a result of this decision of the government?
Quite simply, with so many people out of work and so many businesses failing, tax revenue obviously will not be as high as was expected even six months ago. There will be $595 million less in personal income taxes coming in for 1982-1983 than was projected back in November. This will be in spite of the fact that personal taxes will be increased by $160 million in 1982 because of the deindexation provision introduced in the last budget.
In seven months the projected revenues for 1982-1983 fell $6.4 billion while expenditures increased $2.6 billion. That is the kind of tragic situation in which Canadians find themselves today.
May l call it six o'clock and return after the dinner hour, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, earlier today a number of members referred to the Minister of Finance as a baseball player, to their experiences in baseball, to the fact that he had been up once and struck out, up twice and struck out, up three times and should be out of the ball game, and so on. Upon reflection, although I played ball in my youth, I think a more appropriate game would be hockey. I remember watching a hockey game last winter. I will not mention the teams because what I am
about to describe is something of which I am not particularly proud. Half way through the hockey game, one player who was particularly rambunctious found himself encouraged to jump up into the stands and start beating someone over the head with his hockey stick. It was a fan who had aggravated him. Eventually the player was thrown out of the game. I suspect that that probably describes the Minister of Finance more aptly than a baseball player. He is up today with his hockey stick bashing Canadians over the head and is about to be pulled out of the game, if Canadians had an opportunity to make that decision today via a federal election.
Today we are debating Bill C-125, a bill to give the government the authority to borrow $11 billion. It must be seen in a certain context. When the Thirty-second Parliament first began, the government eventually came to Parliament asking for permission to borrow $12 billion. At that time many difficult questions were asked about how the money would be spent and so on, and hesitantly approval was eventually received. A few months later the government said that it needed another $14 billion to continue on because it was a little short; its revenues were not as much as its spending. The government needed authority to borrow another $14 billion. Then a little later it came before us again and asked permission to borrow $6.6 billion. That $6.6 billion request just received royal assent on June 17. Today, virtually four weeks later, the government has the audacity to come before Parliament and say, "Listen, we have erred in our judgment. Things have not gone quite as we expected. We are not asking for $6.6 billion this time. We are asking for $11 billion". It is asking for $11 billion only four weeks after the last request. If that does not describe a government which is out of control, if that does not support the Auditor General's claim that the economy is on its knees or the previous auditor general's comments that we are going down the tubes, I do not know what does. The government has had to come to Parliament to seek authority to borrow $43.6 billion because of its misjudgment and mismanagement of the economy. It is a sad state of affairs in the wealthiest country in the world.
If positive things had occurred as a result of this borrowing, that would have been one thing. I do not think that we can consider a 60 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies in the first six months of this year as any kind of positive program. I do not think we can consider the 37 per cent increase in business bankruptcies as any kind of positive program. I think we should be ashamed when we learn that plant capacity in the country is operating at 69 per cent of its capacity. That means there is a 30 per cent idleness in the factories of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been a member of this House for a little over eight years, and I am used to the show of rhetoric displayed by members of the New Democratic Party. Our friends on the left of the Canadian political spectrum are usually very fond of demanding more elaborate social programs, and they obviously tend to favour a more expansionary budget policy. To them, budgetary deficits are not a problem but a routine instrument of the government's economic policies. That is why I was quite astonished when I saw the position being taken by that party on Bill C-125, legislation that will provide the government with borrowing authority for $11 billion. 1 am particularly

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
surprised, Mr. Speaker, since, as the House is well aware, the New Democratic Party has already shown its true colours with respect to Bill C-124, pursuant to which wage increases in the federal public sector will be limited to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. The effect of this policy will be to allow the government to save some $800 million over the next two years. That is why I have some doubts as to the logic of the position taken by the New Democratic Party on Bill C-125 since, if, as they claim, a budget deficit of nearly $20 billion is too high, I am surprised they should take a position that would have the effect of adding another $800 million to the deficit.
As for the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative Party, as usual, it is convinced that by repeating over and over again that the budget deficit is too high and is causing inflation, it will be making a useful contribution to the debate in the House and towards solving our country's economic problems. Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether our friends in the New Democratic Party or in the official opposition have any constructive ideas and any sound and well thought out alternatives.
Only yesterday, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) wanted to set a ceiling of $5 billion on the government's borrowing authority under Bill C-125. Mr. Speaker, I have no objection at all, but 1 would have appreciated it if the Leader of the Official Opposition had used his speaking time in the House to explain which budget items he would cut to manage a reduction of $6 billion in the government's total budget. He should have told the House which taxes would have to be raised and which expenditures would have to be cut. With the exception of some vague references to the National Energy Program and hospitality-related expenditures by senior officials, he mentioned the purchase of briefcases for public servants and finally said that if these budget items were eliminated completely, it would be possible to save about $25 million. Well, that is not going to do much for a $78 billion budget. Predictably, he quickly got on to his favorite subject, namely, the privatization of Crown corporations, and I hope the Leader of the Opposition will recall the reaction he got from Canadians on February 18, 1980, after he started toying with the idea of eliminating a number of Crown corporations which had served our country well for some twenty or thirty years.
Mr. Speaker, there are only so many ways to reduce a budget deficit. In fact there are three ways: increase taxes or reduce expenditures or a combination of the two. So the first question is: Is the Official Opposition in favour of higher taxes? No, of course not. In fact, they are just slavish imitators of the Reaganomists in the U.S., and like them, they tend to favour tax cuts. In fact, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that, since the budget was brought down on June 28, they condemned the 6 per cent ceiling on the indexation of personal tax exemption, which, if inflation remains higher than 6 per cent,
would, of course, constitute a form of tax increase. So a tax increase is out of the question. We may now ask whether they favour a reduction in expenditures, since they do not want to raise taxes. One would think that our friends in the Official Opposition would be in favour of a reduction in expenditures. Not so, Mr. Speaker, and except for a few vague references 1 mentioned earlier and which were made yesterday evening by the Leader of the Opposition, the latter has no definite or detailed proposals regarding government programs that could be cut-and justifiably so in some cases-in order to reduce the government's expenditures. Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brought down his budget on June 28, he proposed a ceiling on the indexation of various social programs, more specifically family allowances and old age security. For the government, this would mean a $360 million reduction in expenses. How did they react? The next day during question period, the New Democratic Party members and members of the Official Opposition accused the government of fighting inflation by exploiting low-income groups in our society.
Mr. Speaker, at this point I want to set the record straight, because the members of the opposition have been mouthing worse than half-truths, they have been practically telling falsehoods about this question. As far as old age security is concerned, is a government that, starting in 1983, will put a ceiling of 6 per cent on increases in old age security benefits, is such a government using these people as hostages in its fight against inflation? The facts are simple enough. Among the elderly, 47 per cent receive only old age security benefits, that is, they receive no guaranteed income supplement, and in their case it is true that if inflation were to remain at 11 per cent- which is far from certain, since 1 think the measures taken by the government should, in the months to come, bring about a substantial drop in inflation levels-but assuming that inflation remains at 11 per cent, Mr. Speaker, for the 47 per cent of Canadians who are not eligible for GIS because they have other sources of income, that would represent a loss of $55 per year or a little over $1 per week, which would enable the government to create jobs for their children and grandchildren and thus put our economy on the road to recovery. As for the 53 per cent who, in addition to the base pension, also receive GIS, they will continue to have their benefits and pensions completely indexed, so that in their case, the 6 per cent and 5 per cent policy will not apply.
Now a few words about family allowances. There are basic allowances which all families receive, and there is also the child tax credit that is received by 70 per cent of the 3,600,000 familes with children in this country. Obviously, in the case of the 30 per cent who do not receive the child tax credit, namely, families with above average incomes, they will have to do without a certain amount, which may vary according to the number of children, but average out to $16 per year. I repeat, these are families that belong to the 30 per cent that are
July 20, 1982

financially well-off. In the case of the 70 per cent group, there will, of course, be an average loss of $16 per child annually but, to compensate, the government has announced in the budget a $50 increase in the child tax credit. I think it is clear the government, in this recession, wanted to continue in its role of providing for social justice in this country. Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Official Opposition two things. First of all, I would ask it to act responsibly and tell us once and for all how it would bring down the budget deficit: by increasing taxes or reducing expenditures. I want to know, once and for all, and I am sure many Canadians feel the same way. I also would like to know, Mr. Speaker, what the opposition would feel is an acceptable deficit.
In these circumstances, what would be an acceptable deficit? One of these days members opposite will have to lay their cards on the table and for once come up with constructive suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, what I deplore about this debate on the budget deficit is the fact that they lead people to believe that in itself a budget deficit is unacceptable and is bad for the country's economy, whereas I think one has to be more openminded and discriminating. Mr. Speaker, a budget deficit is not necessarily bad in itself, for it can even be used as an instrument of economic policy. One does not have to be a leading economist to be able to understand a few notions of the Keynesian economic theory. According to that theory, governments can be expected to record budget surpluses when the economy is growing and the unemployment rate relatively low; conversely, during an economic recession such as we are now experiencing and when unemployment is high, too high it is true, governments have to resort to deficit financing.
Why should governments resort to deficit financing in circumstances such as those now prevailing? Simply because the government must take over from the private sector which, given the idle productive capacity and overblown inventories, does not make enough investments to keep the economy on an even keel. In fact, Mr. Speaker, what is a deficit? In our case, it means that the government borrows from Canadians through Canada Savings Bonds, other securities and treasury bonds rather than raise taxes. We ought to keep in mind the fact that the major part of the debt of the Canadian government is money borrowed from Canadians. To put it another way, Mr. Speaker, Canadians owe money to themselves. I suggest there is nothing catastrophic about that. Of course, I will be reminded that, although what I am saying is true, the fact remains that government deficits-and they say this without a shred of supporting evidence-fuel inflation and therefore push up interest rates. Well now, Mr. Speaker, let us see if that is true. Is there any way to show that there is indeed a link between the level of government budgetary deficits on one hand, and the rates of interest and inflation on the other?

Let us compare Japan and Canada. As everybody knows, Japan's current inflation rate is a shade over 3 per cent and its rate of unemployment is roughly the same. And yet, Mr. Speaker, during the six-year period between 1975 and 1981, year in and year out the budgetary deficit of the Japanese public sector has always accounted for a larger share of their gross national product than was the case in Canada. In 1975, Mr. Speaker, it was 2.8 per cent in Japan and 2.5 per cent in Canada. In 1976, 3.8 per cent against 1.7 per cent in Canada. In 1977, 3.7 per cent against 2.4 per cent in Canada. In 1978, 5.5 per cent against 3.2 per cent. In 1979, Japan's public sector deficit was 4.8 per cent of the gross national product compared with 1.9 per cent in Canada. In 1980, 4.2 per cent against 2.1 per cent and, in 1981, 4 per cent against 1.2 per cent. I might also mention the borrowing requirements of the governments, the percentage of the gross national product, and make a comparison between Canada and Japan. In 1980, Japan's public sector borrowing requirements amounted to 10.8 per cent of the gross national product.
In Canada, the figure was 4.5 per cent. We can do the same for 1979: 10.6 per cent for Japan compared with 4.4 per cent for Canada. Mr. Speaker, since we know the rate of inflation in Canada and in Japan, I think we also know that it is difficult to find a relationship between budgetary deficits on the one hand and the rate of inflation and the level of interest on the other.
Let us make another comparison, Mr. Speaker. It has become popular in the last little while to compare Canada with the United States, our powerful neighbour to the south. In 1981, the government deficit represented 2.4 per cent of our GNP. In the United States, the budgetary deficit of the federal administration amounted to 2.1 per cent of the GNP. For all practical purposes, the difference was therefore minimal, Mr. Speaker. Yet the rate of inflation in Canada is still something over 11 per cent compared with 6.5 per cent in the United States. What we may conclude from this, Mr. Speaker, is at the very least that no one can establish a relationship between government budgetary deficits and levels of inflation and interest rates. The situation in Japan proves this very clearly and very definitely, as does the comparison between Canada and the United States for the year 1981.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that because of the very high level of savings in Canada-as we all know, nearly 14 per cent of the available personal income is now invested in savings in Canada-the deficit of just under $20 billion can be financed without putting any upward pressure on interest rates. Nevertheless, we must remember one thing, namely that businesses and the government compete to a certain extent on the money markets, and 1 believe that we should look very closely at the possibility of using the tax system to make businesses much less dependent on the money markets so that they can generate their own investment sources through their own profits. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the present situation, it is

July 20, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
time to review very closely the possibility of abolishing the taxes on corporate profits and of taxing these profits when they are transferred to shareholders as dividends. Of course, some will say that this would encourage businesses not to pay out dividends and to reinvest instead, but in my opinion, it would be a marvellous invitation to reinvest and it would make businesses much less dependent on the money markets. This would mean less upward pressure on interest rates, but I think it would also have the very beneficial result of increasing significantly the value of corporate shares and the loss of earnings by shareholders because fewer dividends would necessarily be paid out. This would be more than compensated by the significant increase in the value of shares. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, this would tremendously encourage reinvestments, especially in the case of small and medium-size businesses which would have the choice of distributing dividends that would be taxable or of simply reinvesting their profits, thus creating employment and contributing to the economic recovery, a great advantage to the Canadian population as a whole. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we would have to consider other factors as well. I am thinking in particular of all our business grant programs, many of which I think simply promote inefficiency.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that, with the exception of regional development grants, if Canadian businesses really want to play the game of free enterprise and of the capitalist system, the government should stop paying grants to businesses, so as to cut its spending, of course, although lower corporate profits would certainly affect federal tax revenues. Of course, the implications of such a reform under the capital gains tax system would have to be considered.
Mr. Speaker, while there is no evidence of a cause and effect relationship between government deficits and inflation and interest rates, I believe that it is nevertheless vital for the future of our economy to reduce inflation. Otherwise, we run the risk of finding ourselves with higher inflation and more unemployment than at the present time. It is often said, especially by labour leaders, that the government has overemphasized the fight against inflation and neglected the fight against unemployment, and that by simply inverting these priorities, the government could promote an economic recovery tomorrow, even though this might create a bit more inflation. Mr. Speaker, I find such talk irresponsible because the economy is not so compartmentalized. It is a bit like communicating vessels, and even more so in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Since Canada exports 30 per cent of the goods and services it produces and since two thirds of our exports go to the United States, 20 per cent of all jobs in Canada are directly dependent on our capacity as a country to compete on the American market.
If, because we stopped fighting inflation, we found ourselves with an inflation rate of 15 or 20 per cent, which is not impossible-some Latin America countries have inflation rates of 50
and 100 per cent, and it could easily happen here-it is obvious that labour unions would then call for wage increases of 15, 20 or 25 per cent, which would obviously affect our production costs. As we know that in the United States, with an inflation rate of about 6'/2 per cent, collective agreements are now being signed at 5, 6 or 7 per cent or even less, it is obvious that we would very quickly find ourselves in a noncompetitive position on the American market, and that we would have not only a much higher inflation rate, but also an even greater unemployment problem than at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, I was reading today the comments of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark), and I was struck by his repeated attempts to undermine the anti-inflation policy of the government. Several times in his speech, he mentioned the fact that the government had decided under Bill C-124 to restrict wage increases for public servants to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent in 1984. He made a subtle attempt to undermine that policy. Mr. Speaker, I would like the Leader of the Official Opposition and the members of his party to make up their minds and to have the courage to practise what they preach when Bill C-124 is put to a vote. However, we know that the Leader of the Official Opposition is aware that all the poles show that 50 per cent of all Canadians support our budgetary and anti-inflation policies. Of course, he reads the poles. And we all know that the depth of his beliefs is equalled only by the depth of his political philosophy, which is saying a lot.
In concluding, I would like to say a few words about the need for a new philosophy in the public service if we truly want to reduce the growth rate of government spending. To anyone who is more or less familiar with the public service, how careers are developed and powerful mandarins are made, the system encourages behaviour that is not helpful at all in slowing down federal spending. A young and ambitious bureaucrat, who wants to have a brilliant career and be promoted in a matter of years, must have an increasing number of staff under his direction, and responsibility for increasingly larger budgets. This is one of the criteria used to evaluate our federal public servants and managers, and to determine whether a young or middle-aged public servant should or should not be promoted. Mr. Speaker, I think that in the months and years to come some serious changes will have to be made in this respect. I think that a feeling for sound economic management and financial restraint will have to become a way of life in the federal public service because, otherwise, I feel that we are only fooling ourselves, no matter which party is in power, if we believe that we can actually control the growth of government spending.

I accept that, Mr. Speaker. Let us go on and look at where inflation in Canada stems from. I believe it is government induced and government sponsored. StatsCan, the federal government's own department, has revealed figures which I hope some of the members on the government side and the Minister of Finance will soon have an opportunity to read. StatsCan reports that while all consumer prices rose between May, 1981, and May, 1982, many prices which are controlled or heavily influenced by government rose far faster than those in the private sector. For example, energy costs are up 23.8 per cent and transportation costs are up 16.1 per cent. By the way, transportation costs will rise even further when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) implements his Crow proposal. For the producers of grain in Western Canada these costs will increase about 45 per cent over the next three years and they will double in the next five years. Tobacco and alcohol costs, also controlled by governments, are up 15.6 per cent. But the other components of our economy, those not controlled or influenced by government rose far less. For instance, clothing rose by 6.3 per cent. According to a recent Statistics Canada study, private sector inflation was 9 per cent while the rate for government and government regulated industries was 18 per cent, twice as high as private sector inflation.
What about the postal rate? There was a postal rate increase of 72 per cent. It is not bad to have an increase of 72 per cent if you can have mail delivered to your door and if you can use the new Priority Post. But in my riding of Kindersley-Lloydminster, Saskatchewan, 95 per cent of the people drive to pick up their own mail. They drive 10, 15 or 20 miles one way. They suffered a 72 per cent increase just to get their letters out, but if they happen to go on a Saturday morning, the post office is closed. I cannot see why, when the government is trying to assess the blame for inflation, it does not look within itself and at some of the policies it has brought forward.
We have listened to the Mi lister of Transport speak. Fie stated that Canadians were .poiled and that we had to be pushed into line. We have heard the same thing from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and from the Minister of Finance. To back up my statement, the hon. member across the way, the hon. member for Montmorency-Orleans (Mr. Duclos), said that Canadians are saving. That means individual Canadians are living well within their means. If you can save from your after-tax income, you are not overspending. In 1979, individual Canadians saved 11 per cent of their after-tax income. In 1980 they saved 11.2 per cent; in 1981 they saved
12.4 per cent and in the first three months of this year Canadians saved 13.3 per cent of their after-tax income despite rising unemployment and inflation. That is living well within your means.
I cannot say the same thing for the government. Where is the fairness of imposing dictatorial government policies upon individuals who are saving their own money to protect themselves against the government that runs their country? Canadians are saving because they are scared stiff of what is ahead for them under this government. They want to try to save everything they can so they can be protected from what they see this government doing and what they have seen it do in the past.

The pace picked up in 1978. The corporation bought Pacific Petroleums Ltd. for $1.5 billion, partly out of production earnings and partly out of a further federal contribution of $240 million. It finished that year with a B.C. oil refinery, interest in coal, uranium and various other minerals, minority shares in two pipelines, 426 gas stations and 2,038 employees.

The budget proposes to provide $750 million for job creation. Economists tell us that $1 billion is required to lower the unemployment rate by one per cent through job creation. When I look at the
July 20, 1982

budget, the clear implication is that the $750 million in new spending is not there. At best, there is $267 million of new spending, and at worst there is $117 million allocated for new homes this year in job creation.
There is nothing mentioned in the budget about the tax increases in UIC which will be imposed upon Canadian employers and employees. The implications of that tax could mean that each employee in Canada could pay up to $142.50 more per year for UIC payments. As a group, employers could pay $1.2 billion more this year.
While the government talks about borrowing money, it introduced a budget which increased taxation. Once again this shows the inequity. For example, the 1984 federal and provincial tax increases which will come about as a result of capping indexing at 6 per cent will mean, for a single taxpayer with no dependants who makes $10,000 earned income, a tax increase of 14.7 per cent. However, the single taxpayer who makes $100,000 a year will have an increase of 2.5 per cent. If we take the example of a married taxpayer with two dependants under the age of 18 who has $20,000 earned income, we find that his increase in taxes will be 21.7 per cent. However, a similar taxpayer who earns $100,000 a year will have an increase, under the deindexing that has taken place under this government, of only 3.2 per cent. Is that a just society? It is not just nor is it fair, and the members opposite know that.
During the last election campaign, members of the Liberal Party promised to keep the rate of government spending below the growth in the GNP. The government is spending twice as fast as it promised during the election campaign. Yesterday in the House we heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) give his government's policy on upholding election promises. My colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) asked the Minister of Agriculture what happened to his election commitment for a special structure on farm fuels which would be exempted from federal taxes. At the present time the government takes 60 cents, or 40 per cent, for every gallon of gasoline used in the production of food in the agricultural industry in this country. However, what did the minister say on behalf of his government? He said that the speeches used during an election campaign were not prepared speeches; they were made in the heat of an election campaign. We now hear directly from the minister what many people in Canada are beginning to believe, that the Liberal Party and the government will say anything during an election to get elected. They do not feel any commitment to fulfill those promises.
The hon. member for Montmorency-Orleans spoke about capital gains during this debate. I agreed with some of the points he made about that subject. But the Minister of Agriculture during the 1980 election campaign promised all farmers a once-in-a-lifetime capital gains exemption. It is not there. It is not there for small business and it is not there for farmers. He also promised to provide an option to change the valuation day. We have seen nothing about that. When the hon. member for Vegreville asked the minister how he was

proceeding with these promises, the minister answered that he was coming along slowly.
We have an appointed member in the Senate, from the Province of Saskatchewan, Senator Argue. He is a cabinet member who is responsible for the Wheat Board and he is assistant to the Minister of Transport. After the budget which made this $11 billion borrowing authority bill necessary, he said that Canadians face a confident future. He said that the government has given leadership with this budget, providing a sense of direction and a target for Canadians to aim at. If anyone knows the Senator from Saskatchewan, he is some target.
What was the reaction to the budget? The best indication is investor interest. Share prices plummeted 13.14 per cent on the Toronto Stock Exchange under hectic trading the day after the budget. The day after the other budget in October of 1980 the market dropped 0.89 per cent. After the November budget the market went down 1.99 per cent.
If hon. members want to talk about confidence we should make comparisons with the budget of the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), in the winter of 1979. That budget, which was later defeated by the NDP and the Liberals, caused the market to rise by 1.9 per cent, a rally on the market.
I heard the members from the Liberal Party west, the NDP, talk about how to expand the economy. I would like to draw to their attention some remarks made by the predecessor to their finance critic, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) since he left the House. Mr. Rae began by saying that Ontario's unemployment rate last month was 9 per cent. He wanted the treasurer of Ontario to do what the finance minister in this House had done. He said that he should reassess his policies and bring in a new budget. He wants to double the deficit and tax the corporations. He wants to tax those who have the ability to pay. That is what the leader of the NDP in Ontario wants to do. He wants higher taxes. The reason there is so much unemployment is that we have fewer corporations which are able to employ people. That will not work.
As I draw my remarks to a conclusion I would like to read to hon. members opposite the words of a prominent Canadian stated in 1965. He said: "It must never be forgotten that in the democracies that we know the political party is not an end but a means, not a goal but an instrument. He who enters a political party, then, is choosing a tool. We do not repudiate any of our convictions. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the bill before us today clearly and chillingly illustrates the serious financial problem being faced by this nation. We are deeply in debt, and the interest we pay on that debt pushes us even further in the hole, a hole dug for us by the government with its abysmal fiscal and economic policies and its arrogant and wasteful spending.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Now, be nice.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I am being nice to the minister, or I could say a lot more than that.
Like the sink holes which swallow up everything in their path, the hole created by the government has gobbled up homes, businesses, farms and jobs of thousands of Canadians in every community across the country, in large cities and small towns, and those who have been fortunate enough to own homes are losing them because of high mortgage interest rates which have nearly doubled their monthly payments. Right across the country, businesses, large and small, have been going belly up as business bankruptcies climbed to 5,383 in the first half of this year, 37 per cent higher than the previous year. Experts say that the number of firms going out of business may actually be five times greater than the recorded rate because most of them do not even bother to file bankruptcy. So we may have upwards of 25,000 employers losing their livelihood in the first six months of this year. Given an average of 11 employees per firm, some 275,000 employees will be out of work as a result and will be forced to join the ranks of more than 1.5 million already unemployed. In one way or another, millions of Canadians have toppled into the hole created by the government and thousands more are expected to vanish into the abyss.
The hole created by the government has become a seemingly bottomless pit and, into this bottomless pit, the government would have us willingly toss another $11 billion, just like that, no questions asked, or, if questions are asked, no answers will be given. That is because the government has a history of taking, not giving. What it takes is the taxpayers' money. It then takes more money so that the hole gets bigger and bigger.
Our gross national debt was $119 billion at the end of 198081 fiscal year, and it is expected to reach $135 billion this year. By comparison, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office in 1968, the nation's gross national debt was $31 billion. The government has plunged the country another $104 billion into debt since that time. This gross national debt of $135 billion is equal to a debt of $5,560 for each and every Canadian, or $14,260 for each taxpayer. While the debt itself is shocking enough, the interest we pay on the debt is staggering. The cost of interest on the public debt this year will be $16.6 billion. This is the cost equivalent of $680 for every man, woman and child in the country, or $1,750 for each and every taxpayer. One tax dollar in five is now used to pay interest on the nation's debt.
Faced with these financial horrors, it would be reasonable to assume that the government would be drastically trimming its spending and working night and day to develop and implement policies for rapid and stable economic growth. Not so. The government's June budget forecast a record deficit of $19.6 billion this year, and the estimates are that it will be considerably higher than that. Deeper we go down into the bottomless pit.
The government adds to our deficit, and then finds itself only two options from which to choose to finance that deficit. First, it can print more money, and over the past ten years it has done so to cover up to $12.4 billion of its financial requirements. But putting the Mint's printing presses on overtime eventually just adds to the problem. The more dollars are printed, the less they are worth.
The other option open to the government, that is, to borrow money, is also fraught with financial penalties. In 1981, borrowing by the federal government accounted for 44 per cent of all net new security issues placed in Canada. Borrowing of this magnitude has an obvious effect on the supply and demand for money and, thus, on the interest rates that must be borne by the private sector. Simply put, this means that, with the federal government borrowing almost half the available money, what is left over is limited and costly, which is why interest rates remain so high and why Canadians are being forced out of their homes, forced to abandon their businesses and farms and forced onto welfare rolls as they lose their jos.
It is not that this government cares one whit for the plight of millions of Canadians. It wants the authority to borrow $11 billion and the devil take the hindmost. The $11 billion it seeks permission to borrow will be added to the $3.6 billion in unused authority from previous years, plus the $6.6 billion authorized last June. If the bill before us today passes, it will give the government the right to borrow a total of $21.2 billion, an amount significantly higher than the $17.1 billion financial requirement outlined in the budget.
There is no reason to assume that the bill will not pass. Despite the grief which excessive government spending and continued high interest rates have caused millions of Canadians, no one on the opposite side of the House seems to care about or understand the urgent need to place the welfare of people before political party loyalty, not even when most of them privately cringe over what occurs in their names.
Not one member on the opposite side of the House has risen in his or her seat to condemn publicly the record level of business bankruptcies in the country. Not one member on the opposite side of the House has risen in his or her seat to condemn publicly the financial hardship the June budget will impose on the elderly and low-income families because of increased taxation. Not one member on the opposite side of the House has risen in his or her seat to condemn publicly policies which have resulted in the unemployment of well over 10 per cent of the Canadian work force. Not one member on the opposite side of the House has risen his in or her seat to protest publicly either increased consumer costs or industry failures as a result of the disastrous National Energy Program. Those
July 20, 1982

hon. members opposite are not protesting the questionable and costly air trips, 36,000 in 37 days, taken by public employees out of Ottawa and Canada, or the cost to the taxpayer of ministers' use of government planes to and from their ridings. They are not demanding a halt to the millions of dollars wasted on government advertising, blowing their own horn to the tune of $73 million this year. We do not hear them speaking up on behalf of Canadians when the price of postage stamps more than doubles, with an increase of up to 72 per cent. Not a peep was heard from those on the other side when it was revealed that a staff member of the Prime Minister's office was being sent to the French Riviera at the taxpayer's expense to learn French.
It was not anyone on the other side of the House who bothered to unearth the fact that government spent $5 million on food, liquor and entertainment in the first six months of 1981. Nor did anyone on the other side of the House raise the question of why, during a period between March 1980 and June 1981, government employees ran up taxi bills of $7,000 a day. The total taxi bill for this 15-month period is almost $3.5 million.

speechtext: That's not true.

speechtext:
What do you mean it's not true? I suggest that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) look at the Auditor General's report. Who across the floor rose to object to the fact that during the same period the government spent more than $275,000 a day for telegrams and other message services? Who bothered to wonder why officials at Canada Post, who approved the spending of more than $260,000 on telegrams and other message services, are so determined to prevent other Canadians from using alternative services?
No one on the other side of the House has ever complained about the $65 million spent to date by the metric commission to implement a program which is costing business and consumers literally millions of dollars. Not a whimper of protest was heard from the other side when it was revealed last November that the National Capital Commission had decided to spend $1.4 million to change the colour of its trucks and signs.
I am sure many members will be aware that a few years ago the Department of Public Works decided to change all its signs. Depending on where the sign was located, originally the sign had English on the top and French on the bottom in the Province of Ontario and French on the top and English on the bottom in the Province of Quebec, as it should be. Millions of dollars were spent to change that to a rectangular sign so that both languages would be at the same level. That might have some merit, but not at a time of austerity. That kind of money should not be wasted. It continues on and on.
Then there is the $2,000 it cost the taxpayers for a hearing last September by the Canadian Transport Commission on why a Yukon railway should be given more time to instal
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
warning lights when those lights had already been up and working for a year at the time of the hearing.
It did not seem to bother anyone on the other side when last February Canadian National Railways spent more than $64,000 on advertising to wish its competitor, CPR, a happy birthday. Surely a nice letter from the president of CNR to the president of CPR would have been sufficient, and if he had wanted to send a telegram that, too, would have filled the bill quite well.
Members opposite blushed when it was revealed late last year that the Canadian Unity Information Office was spending as much as $500 to $700 a day to have same-day newspapers from other cities flown to Ottawa, even though one of the papers could have been purchased on the same day at a news stand in a local hotel within five minute's walking distance of the Unity office.
No one opposite bothered to hang his or her head in shame when it was learned that during 1980-81 the government was billed $26.3 million for telephone calls not placed on government rented lines or through government operators. The list of financial follies of this government is as bottomless as the financial holes it has dug.
Those opposite prefer to pretend publicly that none of these scandalous incidents have occurred. Canadians will not hear a word of complaint from those opposite, although in all fairness when the heat got pretty bad in their ridings, several members on the government side stood up and criticized the government and the budget, first the November budget and later the June budget.
A group from the Province of Quebec ten-strong held a meeting and then publicly stated they did not agree with the budget. More recently, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) very truthfully stated publicly that he did not agree with the budget. On his return to Ottawa, he was taken to the woodshed by the Prime Minister, and talked to in a very serious and fatherly fashion. We have not heard very much from him since. Members can smile, but that is true.
