subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING CROWN PREROGATIVE. (B) POWERS OF PRIME MINISTER
EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING CROWN PREROGATIVE. (B) POWERS OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now 13 months since the emergency planning orders passed by Order in Council 1305 were gazetted and legitimized. That was the order in council which drew national attention to the fact that the government was drawing power to itself so that in wartime it would be permitted to build and administer civilian internment camps. What drew national attention to that particular power was the fact that it was being passed at almost the same time as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was being adopted by this Parliament. The government was billing and cooing to the Canadian public and indicating that never again under this new and great Charter of Rights and Freedoms would it be possible to intern people in internment camps.
When that order in council was passed, I think all Canadians would agree, it had the force of law. Yet the government House leader, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), says that that particular order in council has to be legitimized and endorsed by statute in order to give it force and meaning. As I looked at that particular order in council as gazetted, I noticed that directly under the registration number and the date was the heading, "Other than statutory authority". If the government House leader says it needs to have statutory
authority to give it force, but the order in council itself says it gets its force from other than statutory authority, I think that leads us all to conclude that the only other force supporting that particular order in council is the Crown prerogative. The Crown prerogative is an almost mystical term in Canada. In many ways it has been narrowed by statute so that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) cannot in all instances assume dictatorial powers.
I turn now to a letter written by the President of the Privy Council addressed to the two chairman of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments on March 25, 1982. In that letter the President of the Privy Council said:
If Parliament were dissolved, or if the pace of the crisis at hand did not allow the time to assemble Parliament, the government would be forced to act in reliance on the Crown prerogative, to the extent that it provided a legal basis for authority to act.
That was just nine months after the minister said in a speech to his provincial counterparts that if Parliament were not in session at the time an emergency arose the government would have to act extralegally.
In the summer of 1981 the President of the Privy Council said the government would act extralegally. In March he said it would have to rely on the Crown prerogative, which naturally then leads us to ask what the powers of the Crown prerogative are. I therefore wrote to the research department of the Library of Parliament and asked that department to undertake a study on the powers of the Crown prerogative. On April 27 of this year the research department sent me the results of its study. The report is entitled "Emergency Powers: Executive Action in the Absence of Legislation". Nothing could be more to the point than a title like that. I would like to quote what the research department of the Library of Parliament said on page 15 of its report:
Executive action without such legislation is always possible, but has very little legal basis. If a situation arose in which Parliament could not enact legislation, the government would act and the legality of the actions would be later determined by the courts under the common law, unless an indemnity Act were passed.
Those are some very operative terms.
Executive action without such legislation is always possible-
If a situation arose in which Parliament could not enact legislation, the government would act and the legality would be tested later.
My mind flips back to the year 1970 during the so-called Quebec crisis when 450 people were arrested in the Province of Quebec without charges being laid. Those people were never seriously questioned. They never stood trial, and most of them were released later without ever having been charged. It is now 12 years after that event but how many of those people have reached the point that they could legally challenge the government? The fact is that after the event those people are in no position to question the legality of that action; they either feel
July 20, 1982

too harassed or too impoverished to challenge the government. The government has the power to act extra legally under the powers of Crown prerogative and most of the people affected by that extra legal activity are in no position to check things later.
The government has had a full year since this was brought to light to draft legislation but that has not been done. No legislation has been tabled. We have no way of knowing what it will contain. There is no way of limiting the Crown prerogative, so one must conclude that the government does not want to, and certainly that it does not want the Canadian people to know the limitations of the Crown prerogative, if there are any.
The clue may rest in a speech made by the President of the Privy Council a year ago, Mr. Speaker. I should like to quote three paragraphs from it. Ele said:
But there are factors in addition to a concern for human righs that militate in favour of an emergencies statute. When we need authority during a crisis, we cannot afford lengthy discussion about "inherent powers" that may be implicit somewhere in precedent. When we need to act decisively within the law, we cannot afford to be burdened by real uncertainty about the law ...
And if the emergency arises when Parliament itself is dissolved, we would at present have no option but to act extralegally.
Later in the speech he said:
I believe that three general classes of emergency can, during peacetime-
And, Mr. Speaker, 1 underline, "during peacetime".
-threaten the "peace, order, and good government of Canada"-
First, there are emergencies in which the safety and welfare of large numbers of Canadians are threatened. An unexpected, serious shortage of essential commodities such as food or fuel provides one example of such contingencies-
If we think back to the energy crisis of a year ago, we will realize that now we have virtual nationalization of our energy. If we think of the possible emergencies that could arise regarding food, we realize that now we have the Canagrex legislation to deal with that problem. These are the kinds of emergency powers that are ominous for all Canadians, and they need to be dealt with by legislation that will explain clearly what the government is up to with this emergency powers legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING CROWN PREROGATIVE. (B) POWERS OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member already knows the answer to his question, and he knew it before he asked it. The Crown prerogative to which he refers is, according to Dicey:
-both historically and as a matter of actual fact, nothing else than the residue of discretionary authority which in any given time is legally left in the hands of the Crown.
The prerogative amounts to no more than those powers that Parliament and the courts continue to allow the Crown to exercise alone. What remains of the Crown prerogative is a residue of royal discretionary authority following centuries of evolution during which the struggle for the supremacy of parliament was conducted.
Prerogative powers are non-statutory in origin and are always liable to be superseded by legislation. Indeed, the
Adjournment Debate
Crown prerogative exists as a source of legal power in the hands of the executive only to the extent that it has not been abrogated by statute.
Among its other uses, the Crown prerogative in Canada has often been relied on to change or clarify internal working relationships among federal departments and agencies. It has long been established that the prime minister of the day may assign responsibilities to Her Majesty's ministers and alter these to suit changing circumstances, provided this is done in a way which accords with duties specified by legislation.
A recent example of this use of the prerogative was the passage of Emergency Planning Order P.C. 1981-1305. As the hon. member well knows, the order assigns only planning responsibilities to federal ministers in order to enhance our over-all standard of emergency preparedness, and does not purport to convey any new powers to ministers or anyone else.
However, if I understand the hon. member correctly, he is concerned about an allegedly unlimited prerogative power being used to implement the emergency plans called for in the planning order in any time of proclaimed emergency.
In this context, Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat what the minister responsible for emergency planning has already indicated, namely, that no such unlimited prerogative power exists. Some limited authority does remain in the Crown prerogative as it might pertain to great national emergencies, but it is an enormous overstatement to characterize this residue as "unlimited".

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-PROPOSED INCREASE IN LAND RENTS. (B) RENTS CHARGED TO PARK EMPLOYEES
NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-PROPOSED INCREASE IN LAND RENTS. (B) RENTS CHARGED TO PARK EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motto of this Liberal government in Ottawa is, "Don't do as I do, do as I say". The government is capping the wages of its employees and then taking much or all of the increase back by increasing land and accommodation rentals. The government is asking industry to keep prices down, and then increasing the rentals of land and accommodation for its employees. Employees' wages at Banff National Park have been capped at 6 per cent and 5 per cent; at the same time accommodation rentals are being increased for those employees by 15 per cent to 40 per cent, and higher. The continual increasing of prices induces inflation, makes it necessary for employees to bargain for higher wages in order to make both ends meet. The government should practise what it preaches, namely keep prices down in order that wages will not have to rise. But in the case of Banff, and I understand in other national parks, the government is keeping wages down, but putting up the rentals.
In Banff, for instance, in the case of one employee the minister himself stated in a letter, "your payments now constitute 13.1 per cent of your gross income from Parks Canada". The minister also stated in the letter that they have prepared a proposal which would allow the establishment of rents in Banff at approximately 10 per cent above the average

July 20, 1982
Adjournment Debate
rent charged at bordering parks. Big deal! Why should the rents be 10 per cent higher for the employees in Banff who must live there than it is for those who live outside the park? Why must they be penalized because they live close to a place like Calgary where rentals have skyrocketed?
When the minister was answering my question in the House he appeared to be completely confused; he was confusing staff accommodation with commercial accommodation. Did he do that deliberately so that he would not have to answer my question? The minister goes on to say in the letter that the rents are below those charged in the eastern part of the country. I question this very much and I ask him to publish the rentals in national parks in Eastern Canada.
The rental increase of which parks employees have been notified takes effect August 1 this year. The majority of the people there received a $100 rental increase on January 1, 1982, and they are now faced with another $100 increase on August 1. In one case this constitutes a 66 per cent increase.
When an employee is asked to accept wage controls, surely he should be able to expect some rental control as well, particularly when the landlord is the Government of Canada. How can a family live with a 66 per cent increase in rent and receive only a 6 per cent increase in salary the same year? This cannot be done without the family lowering its standard of living or borrowing money. The minister should try it, then he would not be quite so arrogant with his employees.
In the case of another employee, the rent increase required all of his 11.75 per cent wage increase. With the wage restraint of 6 per cent employees will be paying back to Parks Canada-more specifically to Revenue Canada-an even larger portion of their wages. This will leave them less for essentials like food and clothing. Is this being fair to the employees who live in Banff? In other words, this government is fighting inflation on the backs of its employees. It restrains the wages but grabs every cent it can get through rentals and taxes. Surely Crown-owned accommodation should be setting an example to industry if it expects industry to keep its prices down.
The government refuses to recognize the limited land base in Banff, deliberately limited by Parks Canada; and the explosive commercial growth and recreational accommodation demands which have combined to create a situation where affordable alternatives, such as purchasing a building lot or house, or renting suitable private accommodation, is simply beyond the means of park employees.
A survey by the Alberta Government released in February, 1982 indicates a snapshot of prices to enable comparisons between 14 locations. I refer to the item "shelter". Edmonton was set at 100 per cent, and in comparison Banff was 130 per cent; Calgary was 117 per cent, even with all of its skyrocketing prices; Medicine Hat was 72 per cent; Red Deer 101 per cent; Lethbridge 80 per cent; and the Crowsnest municipality 67 per cent. I ask hon. members to note well that Banff was the highest of the 14 places, which even included Fort McMur-ray, at 124 per cent, and Calgary, both of which were thriving until the introduction of the National Energy Program. This
clearly shows the injustice that Parks Canada has and is imposing upon its employees in Banff.
Now with restraint, wage increases are negated by rent increases. In some cases, Parks Canada will take back more than it is giving in the 6 per cent or 5 per cent increases. Employees have virtually been penalized by a government which should be setting an example. Parks Canada has been treating the employees, particularly those in low and medium-wage brackets in Banff, in a servile, arrogant way. Perhaps that is why there is such a heavy turnover of employees in the Banff National Park.
The very least the government should do is to cut the rental accommodation increases to 6 per cent. If it does not do this, it will simply prove that the government wants its pound of flesh irrespective of what it does to inflation and irrespective to what it does to lives of human beings who are working for the betterment of Canada as employees of the Banff National Park.
What I have said about the treatment of the average employee by Parks Canada is even excelled by the gigantic increases imposed by Parks Canada on the commercial and business places in Banff. The Government of Canada has been a government without a heart as far as the Banff area is concerned. Is the government proud of its motto "Don't do as I do. Do as I say"?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-PROPOSED INCREASE IN LAND RENTS. (B) RENTS CHARGED TO PARK EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I reply to the hon. member by assuring him that there will be no general increase in the land rents for Banff for 1982 or 1983. The rents which were set in 1980, are based upon a percentage of the 1979 land value and will remain constant for ten years. The lessees will, for example, in 1989 be paying rent based on this 1979 land value.
The 1980 to 1990 rent is based on percentage of the independently appraised land value. The percentage capitalization rate used is 6 per cent and this rate has remained unchanged for the past two decades.
While the capitalization rate has remained constant, land values in most of the national parks have risen over the past decade, with the result that rents have risen proportionately. Recognizing the needs of residents who are required to live in the parks, the minister offered reduced rents to residential lessees starting in September, 1980. Lessees whose premises are occupied by persons who qualify as eligible residents pay a rent of one-half of 1 per cent of the land value, to a maximum of $250 per year. The hon. member should note that this represents a substantial rent reduction from 6 per cent of land value.
Residential lessees are not the only leaseholders who have benefited from reduced rents. In September, 1980, cottage lessees were offered a rental rate that was reduced from 6 per cent of the appraised land value to 4 per cent. The cottage
July 20, 1982

lessees were offered the choice of phasing in this 4 per cent of the appraised land value over the ten-year period.
The commercial leaseholders have not received the benefits of reduced rents as it is our view and that of Treasury Board that commercial lessees who gain from the private use of public land should pay an economic rent. While the basis of the commercial rent is 6 per cent of the appraised value of the land, the lessee is given the option of phasing in this amount in equal payments over the ten-year rental period. The lessee also has the option of negotiating a rent based on a percentage of the annual gross revenue.
I would like to point out that 6 per cent of the appraised land value has been the basis of rent determination for a number of years. This represents a low return on the use of the Crown's asset and is, in fact, below the capitalization rates charged by other government departments.
The issue of land rents in Banff is quite separate from the issue of rents charged to Crown employees for Crown-owned staff accommodation, such as for a house in a national park. These rates are controlled by Treasury Board and are based upon local market conditions as calculated by CMEIC.
Although Parks Canada can regulate the rents to a limited extent, depending upon several variables concerning the type of accommodation, it still must stay within these parameters. It can only set the rents according to a prescribed schedule given to it by Treasury Board.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-NUMBER OF PROVINCES SERVED. (B) PROVISION OF ONE-DAY SERVICE
CANADA POST CORPORATION-NUMBER OF PROVINCES SERVED. (B) PROVISION OF ONE-DAY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight during the adjournment debate to continue with a question I asked on July 15, 1982 of the minister responsible for Canada Post. The reason for my question at that time was that Canada Post, with many shiny brochures and much glossy paper, announced a new postal service called "Priority Post".
Priority Post consists of two methods. There is Priority Post programmed service which means that a person can have mail picked up on a regular basis, and it can be delivered on a regular basis for those companies and corporations which have a need for that type of service. There is also Priority Post "D" service.
I found it very strange that a Canada Post letter read:
Priority Post . . . now provides next day delivery for your time-sensitive items to major Canadian cities and many countries 'round the world-
It was not too long ago when we expected that. It was called "service"; service by the post office department. It was not too long ago that businessmen and women and operators in cities expected their mail to be delivered when they put it in mailboxes. They expected it to arrive the next day in cities in Canada. In some of those cities, thousands of miles apart, it arrived the next day. That was expected. It was not something special. That is the way they did business.
Adjournment Debate
After a few years the post office came along with those nice red, white and blue mailboxes. They were special mailboxes. If a person mailed a letter by a certain time, it arrived the next day. It was called "next day delivery". That was all done for the price of a stamp. At the time it was 6 cents and then 12 cents. It was expected. Now we have Priority Post which says that it can give next day delivery up to 33 pounds; that it can get it there on time every time.
The reason for my question was that this was Canada Post, which means all of Canada. It means every part of Canada should have access to this type of service. We all pay the same postal rates and the same taxes. The letter continued:
Just bring your important material to a post office counter ... fill in the distinctive Priority Post label provided, for next day "right to the door" delivery in Halifax, Quebec City, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver.
But Canadians cannot use the service in Fredericton, St. John's, Charlottetown, Moncton, Regina, Saskatoon, Prince Albert, Whitehorse or Yellowknife. This is why we have a problem in the country understanding the directions of the government when it comes to serving all Canadians equally or serving them as they should be served. This is why I asked my question.
I find a great deal of difficulty accepting the same 72 per cent increase in the price of postage stamps in my part of Canada but not receiving the same service. I also find it strange that after I asked my question on July 15 I received a communication from Priority Post dated July 20, 1982, which in part read:
"D" service is currently being announced by direct mail to designated centres.
Additional expansion of "D" in Fall 1982.
Why was that information not made available before I asked my question? Why was I not told that Canada Post was considering providing the service to the cities of Regina, Saskatoon, Prince Albert, North Battleford, St. John's, Moncton and Charlottetown? Why was it not explained. I believe there was no intention on the part of Canada Post to serve those other cities in four provinces and two territories. That is what bothers Canadians about Canada Post. Right now in some parts of Canada we understand what other Canadians are going through with the withdrawal of Saturday delivery and Saturday morning closings.
In 1978 a Liberal member, Mr. Mclsaac, who represented Battleford-Kindersley, which is now in my riding, complained to the government about the closing of a post office on Saturday in Rosetown, Saskatchewan. The closure of post offices on Saturday is not a new phenomenon. That is why it is repugnant to people in my part of Canada, as well as to other Canadians, to be treated unequally and not have the same access to Canada Post and to Priority Post and Priority Class D service. I am sure that the parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Schroder) is quite familiar with Canada Post. I await his answer.

July 20, 1982
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-NUMBER OF PROVINCES SERVED. (B) PROVISION OF ONE-DAY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question suggests that the availability of Priority Post in only six provinces automatically excludes the remaining four from the universal postal service. Such a conclusion is based on fala-cious reasoning and shows no understanding of corporate business marketing methods.
Let me explain the expansion of the service to which the hon. member refers. On July 5 of this year, Canada Post launched the first phase of an important expansion of its courier service called Priority Post. Until that date, this special service was available between the cities of Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton and Winnipeg, or between London, Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. The new expansion now makes it possible to send material under 15 kilograms to any of the above cities by Priority Post, as well as to Halifax and Quebec. In addition, several new Priority Post counters were opened in each location.
The hon. member will be pleased that Canada Post has plans, beginning this fall, to provide for another substantial expansion. The next phase of the expansion will see Priority Post being available to all 10 provinces.
Instead of reproaching Canada Post for ignoring some provinces and favouring others, I think the hon. member should compliment Canada Post for its determination to directly challenge some of its more formidable competitors, the
private couriers. The expansion of Priority Post demonstrates that Canada Post can operate boldly, with flair and in a determined manner calculated to maximize its revenues while providing needed and superb premium service to Canadian business.
Canada Post expansion across Canada of this invaluable new service represents a phasing in by stages, a phasing in of a new service based on calculated, sound business practices. Soon Priority Post will be available in all Canadian provinces, but not before Canada Post is ready.
May I remind the hon. member that he has accused the Post Office of ignoring four of the ten provinces. I have already explained this falacious notion. The hon. member, however, did not address himself to Canada's two territories; the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. At present, let me remind the House that Canada Post has no plans to expand to the two territories, but when demand in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories reaches a point which makes Priority Post a viable business enterprise there, Canada Post certainly will consider introducing it there. Canada Post is cognizant of the postal needs of all Canadians.
